Alden Ehrenreich stars as Edward Ridgeway, who’s been ordered to get Highsmith (Helen Mirren) to sign a contract for one more Ripley book or he'll face the unemployment line. Highsmith is predictably highstrung (hah), irritable from the start, and domineering to the end. She wants nothing more to do with the talented Mr. Ripley, the suave sociopath who’s paid her bills for so long and is most known to audiences for being portrayed by a young Matt Damon in 1999. Not one to be deterred so easily, the seemingly naive Edward manages to worm his way into staying for one night at Highsmith’s hideaway house, giving himself time to see if he can pitch the plot for a new novel to the insular author, who may or may not have killed the last hapless employee saddled with the same objective. To say that there’s more to what’s going on here would be stating the obvious, but it would also, perplexingly, be overstirring the pot.

For when Edward and Highsmith reconvene to begin plotting a novel that would excite the author enough to actually write it, A Talent for Murder unspools into what actually takes up the majority of the runtime: a dramatization of the hypothetical book they’re discussing. This story within a story has some parallels to the “real life” plot, what with a young man with more ambition than he lets on charming his way into the life of a woman who’s his ticket to potential profit, and enlists Ehrenreich into a double role by playing the Ripley analogue that Edward and Highsmith are crafting. It’s a neat idea at first glance until you realize that it’s essentially like watching a narrated pitch meeting for the more straightforwardly satisfying thriller that A Talent for Murder wants to be. The metafictional conceit is a double-edged sword that winds up slashing both plotlines, ensuring the “real” story is lacking in suspense and rendering the “fake” story devoid of stakes.

To quote a common meme, the film has 'great gowns, beautiful gowns'; what it's ultimately lacking in, sadly, is surprise.

That’s not to say A Talent for Murder doesn’t have its merits. Mirren and Ehrenreich have solid adversarial chemistry, and the latter acquits himself admirably playing two characters who begin to bleed into each other as the movie marches on. Olivia Cooke proves herself a reliable if somewhat unchallenged performer by the unambitiously written but fancifully named Clementine Balfour, a woman Edward meets on the train into Switzerland whom he mentally recycles into the love interest/con victim of the same name that makes for the second lead of the novel. The location cinematography from frequent Yorgos Lanthimos collaborator Robbie Ryan is gorgeous and colorful, and the film’s costume and production design is first rate. To quote a common meme, the film has “great gowns, beautiful gowns”; what it’s ultimately lacking in, sadly, is surprise.

Despite featuring two plotlines and plenty of room for intrigue, the “story with a story” concept robs the film of urgency. No matter how much murder and mayhem Edward and Highsmith’s character may get up to in his quest for Clementine’s fortune, what is actually happening is two people sitting in a room talking about a novel that does not exist. The multiple layers of abstraction result in a film that struggles to convey the looming dread that drives the best minimalist mystery fare. Typically a movie or play in this style features multiple big twists that completely recontextualize the scenario — think something like Anthony Shaffer’s Sleuth or Ira Levin’s Deathtrap. But A Talent for Murder lacks punch by never having a massive "rug pull" moment to hang its hat on.

With the caveat that I haven’t seen the play this is based on, I can’t help but feel that a significant contributor to A Talent for Murder being too leisurely for its own good is a playwright who is too precious about adapting her own material. Although this is not Murray-Smith’s first film credit, she’s not a screenwriter by trade, having spent much more time in the world of theater. The energy required for a great mystery film is similar but not identical to that needed for a compelling stage play, and that mismatch of form is the biggest anchor holding the film back, even if it’s not enough to sink it entirely.

items.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Review
items.author: jon Burgess
items.content:
Extraction shooters can feel a little like a modern trend, with some heavy hitters like and shaking the table within the last year or so, but they’ve been a growing experiment in the shooter space for the past decade or so. Call of Duty dabbled in it with the original DMZ back in 2022 (you could even argue they were late to the party by then), and its return in 2026 is timely. I’ve logged quite a few bootsteps through the bombed out streets, scattered woodlands, and high security bases of this big new mode over the last week, and after hours of vehicle hijacking, SAM site hacking, and target elimination, I can say this bigger, better DMZ is a welcome newcomer to the extraction shooter slate.

The PvPvE dynamic of extraction shooters often lives and dies by how well the mission and level design encourages you to explore, rewards you for overcoming challenges, and guides you to interact with others in order to keep those spoils. The fictional Korean Hajin region your exploits take place in is well suited for this. Its dense pockets of urban development – a village in the north, the dangerous main city in the east, an isolated prison out west – are separated by rocky forests concealing all sorts of militarized checkpoints and other points of interest hiding loot to shove into your pockets.

Parts of it look a little samey, the consequence of modern urban development where (at least from the outside) most buildings look the same, especially compared to some of DMZ’s big sci-fi competitors that go above and beyond to look striking at first glance. But the map is so big that you could spend the entirety of your approximately half-hour runs in only a fraction of it. And where Battle Royales (like CoD’s own Warzone) move players around by having an encroaching death cloud forcing everyone into a smaller and smaller area, DMZ instead entices squads to adventure with its Dynamic Operations.

Dynamic Ops are spontaneous missions that appear as you travel across the battlefield which come in lots of forms, from securing a package to blowing up a target to escorting a VIP. Many of them are multi-stage affairs that have your fireteam moving from point to point as NPC enemies ramp up a more coordinated defense against you. These all get rewarded by supply drops that grant you loot, the value of which escalates based on how many of them you successfully complete. I prefer this sort of objective chasing to the more standard task lists in other games like this (which also exist here, in fairness) because it makes for more engaging individual runs. I’ll prepare the best I can beforehand, but can’t be ready for every possible string of operations once I deploy.

There are many actions and events, like aforementioned supply drops, that are broadcast to everyone within earshot, hypothetically to tempt other players to be nosy (and potentially belligerent). Despite those lures, open skirmishes with others have been pretty limited, as I’ve found most people opt to mind their own business. The influx of players at launch hasn't really changed the main emphasis on the E in the PvPvE structure of these runs, though human enemies can regularly play spoiler to otherwise solid runs if you’re not diligent.

There was a base level of tension with every step I took or round I let off.

It would be a mistake to confuse passivity with pacifism – this isn’t the Arc Raiders playerbase, which spent many of the opening months of that game more interested in helping than hurting. Whenever another player was in eye or earshot, it was assumed that a firefight was to follow, even though there is a specific truce ping that allows you the extend the olive branch to other players who you know are around but can’t (or don't want to) see in person. Like in all extraction shooters, the most tense PVP moment in DMZ happens when you’re waiting for your ride home and other players have decided that the extraction heli isn’t big enough for the both of you.

Hajin is a pretty lively place. Enemy patrols speed down roadways, sometimes as lone jeeps and other times in large caravans. Helicopters and drones streak across the sky looking for interlopers like me, or occasionally other NPCs from rival factions tearing the map apart. A train runs on a schedule, and you can absolutely hitch a ride on it to get from place to place. Squads of enemies could be posted up anywhere. Weird exploding robot dogs can sniff you out as you slink from building to building. There was always at least a base level of tension with every step I took or round I let off, because there was just enough going on around me that any push I made could be the one that knocked over the house of cards I was hiding behind.

Clashes with the NPC denizens of the DMZ start pretty tame, but ramp up as you and your squad make yourself more notorious by killing enemies and completing objectives. As enemy units start to don armor, pull up in more durable vehicles, and use higher grade weaponry to take you down, firefights can get desperate quickly. There's an instinct for people in pick-up groups to run out on their own, potentially to get first dibs on loot perhaps, and they almost always regret it – it doesn’t take much for enemies to get the drop on you, as you are only where you are and they are potentially anywhere and everywhere else.

Lieutenants are high-level boss challenges that really stand out as maybe the single most difficult thing you can attempt during any given run. They exist in specific regions, but where one in the forests lies in wait for unsuspecting operators to pass through their zone before springing their assault, another is dressed head to toe in armor with a mini-gun and will roam a piece of the city in hopes to stop you mid mission. They are better off avoided unless you’ve brought high-end gear with the specific purpose of hunting them.

The secret sauce of what makes the extraction shooter so appealing is the level of agency each player has to play how they want in a higher stakes PvP setting. You can go into every encounter guns blazing, or you can tip toe through them, taking the long way and hopefully having your patience and preparation rewarded. You can make racking up “objective completes” and bagging top tier loot your mission, or you can try to hunt down every human player you can. I like engaging in a bit of PvP, but my nearly 40-year-old eyes and reflexes frankly can’t keep up with the kind batshit action that goes on in the standard multiplayer modes (or even Warzone). In contrast, DMZ has created a great sandbox that serves all varieties of playstyles adequately.

There's always a way to jam up sightlines or to find some cover and take a breath. Every building has multiple points of entry, so sieges or chases through them always require some level of decision making. Sub-missions are always an option, where you can hack a tower for a UAV scan or SAM site coverage to support you in your main objective, but only if you’re willing the take on the added risk. I always felt like I could “yes, and” what was happening at any given moment, and thats not true for many of DMZ’s contemporaries.

Call of Duty’s top tier military shooter gunplay feels at home in DMZ.

Call of Duty’s top tier military shooter gunplay, toeing the line between the lethality of simulations and the snappy speed of arcadey romps, feels at home in DMZ as well. All of the new tweaks, like the way your weapons interact with your surroundings or movement adjustments, feel like they had roaming gunfights in an open world in mind. Being able to cancel out of mantles so you aren’t stuck in an animation when you least want to be feels like the kind of quality of life inclusion that Warzone demonstrated was needed for a long time. That said, the smattering of guns lack much in the way of real identities outside of the normal archetypal framings that have existed in gaming forever (shotgun, assault rifle, sniper, etc.).

You can also drop into story missions, which are quest chains that include more structure, resembling the campaign missions without the more cinematic story elements. These were pretty rowdy and unique, like an escort mission where our squad had to wheel an injured general out of a hospital, bed and all, while enduring swarms of enemy combatants. There's a finite number of these and the possible rewards are more limited, with less incentive to explore the places around you and no enemy players to pirate or evade. But they serve as a great tasting platter of the pace Dynamic Ops keep and a good tour of the various locations on the map you'll need to get familiar with.

In between missions, you’ll tend to all of your gear and progression from the safety of your FOB. Weapons, crafting ingredients, and consumables that you procure out in the field can be sorted through here, all of it put at risk when you equip it and redeploy. When you unlock the 3D printer and gunsmith areas, crafting new toys and upgrading weapons becomes the main way you spend your plunder to enhance your chances in Hajin. You can easily blow tens of thousands of won to trick out a weapon, but I found that the investments can be worth it in order to differentiate playstyles, like if you want a quieter load out with suppressors or a certain sort of optics to make mid-to-long range encounters more beneficial. I didn’t find the more money I invested automatically made my loadout feel more powerful, though.

Gaining experience is pretty easy as everything you do in the field gives you some amount of it. Progressing through the account level unlocks list was pretty breezy at first, helpful because a lot of recipes for some core equipment like grenades and ammo boxes are early rewards. At around half way up I found things slowed down quite significantly, but I also didn't find many late level goals to be enticing enough to turn up the grind. There's powerful kit, like a pistol that you can shoot downed teammates with to revive them, but I'm not torching all my spare time to sprint to level 64 to get it.

Similarly, Operators have individual sets of trait trees that you upgrade with points they earn in the field. These don’t appear to be novel to any individual fighter; there's no Ghost-specific ability where he gets unique buffs while saying something very British. Instead there are pools of passive traits across three categories, all operators have a choice between the same handful of major traits, and the 15 or so minor traits that fill out the trees are randomized. What makes an operator special seems to be limited mostly to how they look and sound, which was a bit of a bummer.

I was never champing at the bit to get my build “right.”

These traits can be meaningful in the field, though. One of the randomized traits I acquired for Valeria, Ammo Scavenger, doubled the ammo I got from ammo packs and made conserving my shots basically a thing of the past. The faster revive speed all operators have access to in their Survivalist tree has been the difference between clutch plays and total wipes on more than one occasion. There's definitely some kind of character building to be had here, but you really can’t know where it’s all leading until the next group of traits to choose from are revealed. And all that is before accounting for the fact that there's no way to reset or reallocate these trait points outside of abandoning the operator all together if you fail to extract with them (as opposed to spending some cash to get them back into the fight).

All of this created an environment where I was never champing at the bit to get my build “right.” Everything I picked worked at least a little bit. But I was also pretty detached from the whole process once I realized you really only had one shot at it per operator. I haven't maxed out any operator skill trees or account level reward path yet, but there are no substantial carrots left to tempt me down them either. Regardless of the trait investment, how good or bad I did in a run came down to how few bullets I ate in the process, and these trees, though valuable in specific cases, really didn't change that.

items.title: Clayface Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Clayface opens in North America on October 23 and internationally on October 21.

It takes the film a while to find its groove, but once it does, delivers just the sort of nasty but fun I was hoping it would.

Director James Watkins has fashioned a gritty throwback to not only the hardboiled revenge thrillers and low-budget horror flicks of the ‘50s and ‘60s but also to the cult classics of the ‘80s and ‘90s that paid homage to them. (Shades of The Fly, Darkman, and Johnny Handsome can all be found in Clayface.)

Based on the DC Comics character and working from a screenplay by and Hossein Amini, Clayface follows rising young movie star Matt Hagen (), a Gotham City native whose sketchy, hardscrabble background calls to mind that of Mark Wahlberg. Now a successful film actor, everything is going Matt’s way — until he runs afoul of Gotham’s most vicious and powerful crime lord, Markos (David Dencik), whose goons carve up Matt’s pretty boy face as punishment.

Disfigured and distraught, Matt finds no recourse from either the law or from multiple surgeries until he seeks out assistance from Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie). Caitlyn’s similarly down on her luck, with her cutting edge research having been recently ripped off by her former partners. When Matt comes to her volunteering to be a human test subject for her experimental, AI-infused nanobot regenerative tech, she reluctantly says yes. All seems to be going well at first, but this movie ain’t called Clayface because Matt’s new skincare regimen worked out great.

Harries has a young Malcolm McDowell quality to him, as in impish good looks that hint at an inner darkness. The actor never overplays his scenes despite there being plenty of opportunities for him to have gone big. As sympathetically played by Ackie, Caitlyn is more misguided than mad scientist despite being responsible for the physical monster Matt becomes. But while her nanobots have infiltrated and altered Matt, the film suggests they’ve merely unlocked and amplified a very bad side of him that was already there.

When Matt’s pursuit of his attackers and those who have betrayed him finally comes, it allows the film to finally embrace its inherent absurdity and capitalize on the nastiness it was keeping at bay while it was trying to make Matt sympathetic. Once Matt is no longer the victim and becomes the gooey Angel of Death we’ve been waiting for, the film gets a newfound jolt of energy and unleashes some of its most clever, thrilling and darkly funny sequences (following the earlier seen in trailers and a creepy sleep study sequence).

Watkins has previously helmed genre films like The Woman in Black and Speak No Evil, in addition to the iconic “Shut Up and Dance” episode of Black Mirror. He and his creative team — including cinematographer Rob Hardy, production designer James Price, editor Jon Harris, Makeup Designer Nicole Stafford and Legacy Effects — make great use of Matt’s power to shapeshift, but also find the humor and tension in those situations, with Matt using his skills as an actor to literally inhabit a slew of different characters one after another.

As Matt’s condition worsens and his desire for revenge fully consumes him, he devolves morally and physically into something truly monstrous. Clayface’s comics and cartoon-accurate final form isn’t revealed until the film’s closing moments, but it effectively caps off Matt’s tragic downfall.

Although it carries the banner of James Gunn’s DC Studios, Clayface could just as easily have been set outside of the DCU. Aside from taking place in the DC Comics locations of Gotham City and Coast City, there’s nothing on display here that screams DC Comics. Still, Clayface proves that can offer more than just superhero fisticuffs and save-the-world plots. The question remains how large of an audience there will be for them.

items.title: We Build LEGO Hubble Space Telescope: a Miniature Homage to Cosmic Discovery
items.author: Matthew Adler
items.content:
LEGO partnered with NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), the two agencies responsible for building the Hubble Space Telescope, to create an accurate replica commemorating the 35th anniversary of its launch. You can purchase the LEGO Hubble Space Telescope now from Amazon and the LEGO Store.

LEGO is no stranger to making space-themed sets, with plenty of other NASA replicas available including the massive Artemis Space Launch System and the Mars Rover Perseverence, as well as sets based on popular space franchises like Star Trek and the recent Project Hail Mary. But, what I really want is for LEGO to bring back some of the classic 90's space sets like Exploriens and Spyrius – those were the best.

LEGO Hubble Space Telescope is built in three major sections spread across nine bags: the stand, the back portion that houses the instrument bay, and the narrower shaft on the front. This was a very relaxing set to put together, and pairs rather nicely with a space-themed synthwave playlist.

You begin by putting together the stand on which Hubble will be displayed. Unlike most LEGO stands, this one uses some interesting techniques with interlocking Technics pieces to create an angled post that allows the Hubble to "dock" when it's on display, helping to stabilize the unit.

At the base of the display are three translucent printed pieces depicting some of Hubble's most iconic Deep Field images: Pillars of Creation, the Whirlpool Galaxy, and the Butterfly Nebula. These are some of the coolest unique pieces I've seen LEGO make, and they look great integrated into the stand. It also includes a small plaque (which is unfortunately a large sticker on a flat piece) on the side of the support arm that provides information about Hubble, including its overall dimensions, weight, launch date, and the dates of key service missions.

While building this set, I actually learned quite a bit about the Hubble and its inner workings. Over the last three decades, it has recorded more than 1.7 million observations of our universe, producing some absolutely stunning imagery, as it circles in low-earth orbit. The instruction manual includes quite a few interesting facts about the Hubble Telescope, as well as a diagram of all of the scientific instruments recreated inside this LEGO model.

After finishing the stand, you move onto what is arguably the most important section of the Hubble: its large bottom half that houses many of its critical systems and instruments. While I expected this portion to be interesting to put together, it was fairly repetitive, as it's a lot of symmetrical sections and repeated instructions.

It didn't help that much of what I was putting together wasn't recognizable. If it weren't for the diagram in the instruction manual, I would have no concept of what I was building until the outer panels were attached. After all, most of the important components of the advanced camera and spectographs are represented by just four brown corner wall panel pieces.

Because each side is nearly identical, it's easy to get the orientaton mixed up if you're not careful. I think this is why LEGO added (what seemed to be) a random green piece on only one of the sides to help ensure you don't misplace any pieces.

After building the interior and some of the instruments, you add the panels to three of the four sides. The final side is intended to be removable, so you can look inside the bottom section and see the camera, mirrors, sensors, and baffle.

Building Hubble's upper shaft is mostly just putting together four long outer panels. Like the bottom half, the outer paneling is mostly rounded grey pieces and can get quite repetitive. These panels are all long and not very thick, so attaching them to the rest of the build requires some tact, as pressing too hard can cause them to break apart.

One interesting portion of the upper section, though, was the suspended secondary mirror, which clicks into to the panels as they are attached. These panels also lock into one another in a very satisfying way. Additionally, there's a single removable panel here that allows you to peek inside at some more of the components.

At the very end of the upper shaft is the aperture door, which features a hinge that allows you to open or close it, just like on the real Hubble Telescope.

Once the two halves of the Hubble's body are put together, all that's left is the finishing touches. This includes attaching the two communication antennas, which can be folded down or extended and rotated in any orientation, as well as building the two large solar arrays.

Thankfully, the solar arrays aren't giant stickers, as I feared when I saw the initial photographs of this set. Instead, they are thin plastic sheets with the printed solar panels on one side, and shiny silver on the back. Once attached to the telescope's body, they can be easily articulated to face any direction.

The entire time I was putting this set together, I kept wondering just how it was going to rest on the stand. It turns out, there's a small hole in the center of the body that the stand inserts into. But, because this set is a bit top-heavy, it can be slightly wobbly when on the stand when it's not stationary.

Overall, the finished product looks great on display. LEGO did an excellent job recreating the Hubble Space Telescope's iconic design and this set is a must for space enthusiasts.

LEGO Hubble Space Telescope, Set #11382, retails for $139.99 and is composed of 1,252 pieces. It is available to purchase from Amazon and the LEGO Store.

Matthew Adler has written for IGN since 2019 covering all things gaming, tech, tabletop games, LEGO, and more. You can follow him on the site formerly known as Twitter

items.title: Slow Horses Season 6, Episode 6 Review — ’Judgement Day’
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 6, Episode 6, which is streaming on Apple TV now.

The Slow Horses always find themselves in dire situations in season finales. To that end, the closer of Season 6 is no different. They’re chased and hunted and shot at again and again. They scheme (well, Gary Oldman’s Jackson Lamb does) to save their behinds — remember, Moscow rules. Reece Nesmith (Lenny Rush) gets his hero moment, pulling off a Chekov’s harpoon. In a moment of stillness, River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) has it out with his dear old dad, Frank Harkness (Hugo Weaving), who might have a soft spot for his son after all. The mess with the Russians closes with Clayface Jane (MyAnna Buring) dead and MI5 handing over a fall guy that isn’t Sid Baker (Olivia Cooke, who shamefully only gets three seconds of distant screentime this episode).

And yet, even with the endless game of survival the agents play against their agitators, this finale doesn’t feel particularly novel for a series that has given us 11th-hour twists and feel-bad yet satisfying endings for its five prior seasons. Yes, it closed on a huge cliffhanger that sets Slow Horses up for Season 7 (due out next year — get those theories cranking about what, exactly, took River down), but it was all just a little too clean and conventional in a show that has typically embraced the mess.

To neatly tie up all of the loose ends, the show had to make a few leaps. The most egregious is Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas, who nevertheless has given a fantastic performance all season). It’s a bit of a stretch to believe that Diana, after an entire season of quadrupling down on denials and obfuscation, would finally decide to come clean and admit to treason, and even more of a stretch to think that Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) would be the one to convince her how to play it. It was hardly surprising, although nonetheless satisfying, that Damien Cantor and Peter Judd were made to be patsies for the Russians essentially financing a hit on their own soil, but it was somewhat curious at how easily the Home Secretary accepted Diana’s finger pointing as fact. It still seems Diana will face some consequences, based on the teaser for next season which seems to be Shirley (woohoo!) and Ho-centric, but one would think an accusation of treason would come with a heftier investigation rather than just taking the First Desk at her word.

Cantor (Harry Lloyd), in retrospect, was a somewhat disappointing bad guy. In the end, he only mattered in the context of giving the main characters a headache for a couple days. He never showed off his media influence, aside from one viral interview and that he could eat dinners in fancy restaurants alone. We never get a sense of how his news outlet operated in society, though there were plenty of inferences to be made, of course, but Slow Horses has never shied away from being explicit with an antagonist’s ugliness. Even just last season, Ho’s honey trap and her Libyan terrorist group, seeking revenge for Britain’s heavy hand in their country’s destabilization, had far richer characterization. Here, Cantor was a fairly one-note villain-of-the-season (he barely even speaks during his first appearance in Episode 1), motivated by winning a Russian media distribution contract that was mentioned in a single scene.

Pivoting to the rigamarole of Slough House, their chilling at the posh safehouse by Harkness and his goons. Their flee-and-hide routine in the final showdown in Diana’s holiday home and along the lakeshores has its share of exciting moments. (Also, how the hell did River find his way there?) Having them break off into teams was functionally necessary for these scenes, but the compartmentalization often impacted the momentum of things and came off like a stop-and-start game of fight tactics. No offense, but I don’t want Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave in my TV show, thanks. But RIP Emma Flyte (Ruth Bradley), gone too soon but sticking by her word to be the group’s distraction. Louisa Guy (Rosalind Eleazar) also had a scary brush with mortality, but it also wasn’t hugely surprising to see her alive by the end; it would have been too much to kill her off, even for Slow Horses.

The most interesting revelation from that sequence was the curtain-pull on Harkness’s motivations. From that came an actual moment of uncertainty: if he would still go and kill Reece after Cantor called him off. He holds himself to the terms of the job after all. Harkness might have explained away killing Jane as an act of stopping the dangerous pursuer, but it certainly felt bigger than that as he offered River a drink in the aftermath of it all. River letting him get away bookends that short interaction in a meaningful way (and now the show can still deploy Harkness in future seasons).

The last scene back at River’s grandad’s house — where, in a sweet gesture, Sid kept her promise from the last episode, leaving a light on for River — was almost a lovely moment for an agent who’s had a terrible last few days. That final scene of River going for tea, then wine, then collapsing raises a ton of questions, of course. There’s the paranoia around Sid: Did she lure him there? Is she bad after all? More likely, I think, Jim and Jane planted something on one of the objects he touched, knowing that he would return to the house and getting their job done from beyond the grave. Jim did grab the crowbar in Episode 3 when they first broke into the house, and River made a whole show of the residue when he grabbed it. But that seems too obvious. Even though Season 6 laid its tracks maybe too bare, I’m still prepared to be made a fool by Slow Horses again.

items.title: One Piece: Grand Gourmet Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
When it comes to translating One Piece into a video game, developers have typically taken the action route, leaning on flashy battles and wild Devil Fruit powers as pirates sail the high seas. That makes One Piece: Grand Gourmet’s Sanji-centric restaurant builder with the full roster of characters from across the series is an inspired choice. But while I adore the premise and appreciate revisiting the major locations and feeding nearly every character, working to win over residents of the Grand Line often feels as shallow as the lovestruck chef it's based around.

After a storm separates them from the rest of the crew, Sanji and Luffy find a restaurant ship being terrorized by a group of fake Straw Hat pirates who are posing as (and giving a bad name to) the restaurant of Sanji’s mentor, the Baratie. The duo sets sail to beat the fakers in culinary battles and clear the Baratie's name throughout the Grand Line and beyond. Taking a chronological path from the early Romance Dawn days in the East Blue all the way to a taste of the latest arc in the manga and anime, Grand Gourmet is packed with fan service in lieu of a meaningful original story. While I wish there was more meat on the bone, I enjoy Grand Gourmet embracing Sanji’s ethos that everyone who needs food will be fed, and it turns out, everyone the Straw Hats ever met is hungry.

Your floating restaurant starts small and empty, with only a kitchen, a table, and Sanji’s chef skills to cook for hungry customers. Feeding people brings in valuable cash you can use to build out the restaurant with more tables, attractions, and decorations to improve the space's comfort. The more comfortable the accommodations, the happier the customers, and the more they will spend on food. Ironically, comfort is an unfortunate word for this metric. The crimes I must have committed to the concept of interior design have to be the most stressful and sloppy places to attempt to enjoy a meal. I love the idea of building a restaurant that pulls elements from various islands and lets you run wild with the decor, with Sanji cooking delicacies from across the globe, but that tantalizing proposition falls flat in execution.

Each new region brings a set of restaurant fixtures themed to the current story arc you’re sailing through, be that new flooring, lamps, benches, or landscaping. For example, the Thriller Bark set features horror-themed decor, plus a spot to plant the stray zombie friends who accompany the living visitors on the ship. Instead of rewarding you for making an aesthetically pleasing, well-organized dining room, Grand Gourmet doesn’t care about actual comfort. Instead, it incentivizes you to cram every square inch with lamps, benches, and shrubbery to boost stats. Neither Crocodile nor Eustice Kidd ultimately cares what their assigned seat looks like. And because of the limited space and clunky reorganization tools, these areas remained cluttered catastrophes that still somehow made a boatload of money.

Some elements also move beyond the typical restaurant vibe to make the ship a more appealing destination, but they aren’t without their own faults, either. My favorite fantastical attractions are meeting spots for giant sea kings or land crabs, which add cool elements to the ship's deck and showcase the eccentric animal designs of the One Piece world. It’s fun to collect fish to store in an aquarium or keep the pets of visitors in animal-friendly environments. However, once you have the features and creatures in place, there’s not much else to do with them. They’re yet another money-collecting attraction that doesn’t affect their surroundings besides providing a small bump of comfort.

Like the interior design, the restaurant’s food has promising building blocks but lacks the finesse to make planning a proper meal worth the trouble. Sanji draws inspiration from his fellow crewmates and restaurant visitors, letting him make everything from simple dishes like rice or spring rolls to fantastical concoctions based on legendary characters or events from the One Piece world. Piecing together a balanced meal of up to four items lets you sell products at a higher price, and you can increase it further by pairing them with other food endorsed by the same Straw Hat crew member. Except, like the design elements, it’s disappointing that diners are never picky about what you specifically serve them; it only matters that you put the food out.

The best course of action is to serve what’s going to rake in the most cash every time, which the automatic meal tool already does effectively. I wish there were incentives for putting together a regional meal or a group-inspired platter to break up the monotony of only pairing the priciest products. This extends to the fake Baratie boss battles, which put Sanji in a Food Network-esque cooking competition, in which the automatic meals were still plenty successful. You can always put together bespoke plates of food and decorate a meal with different figures, plates, and utensils to spice up the meal-planning experience – there’s just not any reason to do so outside of having a little fun.

Working to win over residents of the Grand Line often feels as shallow as the lovestruck chef it's based around.

Learning to cook new foods is critical to building the restaurant's reputation and fighting fake Baratie, but whether or not you’ll unlock a crucial recipe is a crapshoot. Some foods are key to turning a customer into a fan of the restaurant, which lets them follow you to new regions, but it's nigh impossible to know who might know which recipe. Nothing points you toward who to impress and what food they are capable of inspiring. You have to be lucky enough to have the right items on hand, and the right people on board, to crack a novel recipe. Unlocking a specific food is often dumb luck, and while it can be frustrating to figure out, much of what you need falls into your lap at the right time. The moments when things don’t come together feel bad, though, especially when your favorite characters have to be left behind when the time arrives to move forward on the journey.

While Sanji handles the cooking responsibilities, Luffy sets out to explore with the rest of the pirate crew. The action itself is simple, but I looked forward to searching each new region because it’s one of the few tasks that enables the restaurant to consistently flourish in meaningful ways. These idle activities cost Berry, affinity points, or coins to send the crew to important One Piece islands, villages, and bases – the price is worth it, though, as exploration rewards you with new faces to visit the restaurant, giftable items to create new fans or increase profitability, and precious ingredients for new kitchen concoctions. Some rewards are level-gated while others require a specific crew member to bring them home, giving me a great reason to level up every member of the Straw Hat crew whenever possible (once you’ve found them somewhere in the vast ocean, that is).

Each crew member helps out the restaurant in a way only they can, and these are some of the best realized parts of Grand Gourmet. Sanji, of course, cooks all of the meals; Franky, the shipwright, creates new furnishings and can expand the square footage of the ship; crafty Ussop makes decorations and utensils to modify meals; and the swordsman Zoro trains the Straw Hats, allowing them to level up further for expeditions and other activities. My favorite crew member is the money-hungry Nami, who not only bailed me out financially multiple times but also negotiates a half-price discount on new amenities once a day, giving me a neat loophole to buy expensive ship upgrades on the cheap. Every member of the pirate crew brings a fun element to the ship, even if everything doesn’t necessarily help the cause of beating the fake Baratie.

Running a business isn’t cheap, especially when serving hundreds of hungry mouths in the middle of the briney deep, but I’m disappointed by the lack of pressure or punishment for spending far outside my means. Every shop, buffet, and employee hired to help the cause has daily overhead, which put me deep in financial trouble almost every day. (Don’t get me started on how much it was to add Blackbeard to the payroll.) Each sunrise, my Berry count went negative, and I had to crawl through the day. Because no friction challenged my poor financial management, I never needed to find a better way to run the company. The only time anyone cares how shallow my pockets are is when I'm spending money during the day, and even then, someone usually bailed me out immediately, filling my coffers far more than necessary.

With no reason to think too hard about the business management side of things, what has instead kept me playing Grand Gourmet (even after the close to 20 hours it took me to roll credits) is seeing damn near every single named One Piece character running around the ship and interacting with each other. It’s fun to see old comrades share a table or bitter rivals chat about characters they relate to. Some meetups are surprising and funny, like two villains discussing “work,” which may or may not involve poisoning people with synthetic Devil Fruits. There are also references to its own lack continuity, which make for interesting meetups between characters who may not exist in the same place or lifetime.

Feeding old friends and watching them interact with each other in unexpected ways had me smiling even past the credits.

Each character has an affection rating that, when raised to a specified level, can give your staff new items to craft or more customers to invite, making them important to interact with beyond just the fun of having them aboard. Grand Gourmet looks great too, full of small details on the hundreds of character sprites that are truly impressive. Almost every character’s design is recognizable and unique, with many featuring special animations that bring each person to life, like Akainu firing up a giant magma fist while helping to create a new dish. These flourishes don’t happen often, but do inject some much-needed panache to the normally mundane way everyone strolls around.

While almost every character the anime has produced is here, it’s a shame the same can’t be said for the memorable music, voice cast, or sound effects from its long history. Instead, the soundtrack is limited to a handful of nondescript background themes on a short loop paired with a painfully small sample of sound effects, which makes it feel like an early iOS game (which isn’t a huge shock given this game is so deeply tied to developer Kairosoft’s mobile game lineage). A big part of One Piece’s appeal lies in its audio design and music, so it’s a bummer that Grand Gourmet has none of that.

items.title: Marvel's VisionQuest Episodes 3 and 4 Review: 'Reboot' and 'Malware'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Episodes 3 and 4, which are streaming now on Disney+.

VisionQuest is turning out to be quite the pleasant little surprise. What initially seemed like an obligatory but unneeded follow-up to a loose end from WandaVision is rapidly developing into a series with plenty of heart, soul, and depth of its own. It never pays to count out Paul Bettany's synthetic hero.

Mind you, entertaining as the first two episodes were, my one real reservation with VisionQuest out of the gate was that it was a bit difficult to connect with this version of Bettany's character. As he himself says, he has all the memories of the original Vision but none of his soul. Given how poignant and utterly human Vision was in his past MCU appearances, seeing a cold, aloof, emotionless copy of that character takes some getting used to.

But that problem quickly starts to fade in Episodes 3 and 4. Already, White Vision is making great strides in terms of understanding his emotions and internal conflict and embracing this side of himself he doesn't quite understand. Compared to the Loki series, which basically relied on a quick-and-dirty speedrun to transform the 2012-era Loki (Tom Hiddleston) into something more resembling his post-Thor: Ragnarok self, this feels like a more coherent and purposeful way of bridging the gap between two wildly different versions of an MCU character.

Certainly, Bettany has a lot more to work with in these two episodes, both comedically and dramatically. His malfunctioning processors give the actor some welcome opportunity to deploy a bit of physical comedy in Episode 3. And both episodes make the most of the rapidly deepening bond between Vision and Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica). By all rights, their relationship should feel rushed, but somehow it all works anyway. By the time Vision is coaxing his son on how to reboot him in the hotel swimming pool, he feels well on the road to reclaiming that lost humanity that was so vital to the original character. That process continues in Episode 4, where Vision pointedly stops drawing such a hard distinction between his past and present selves.

I also appreciate how well the show's writers are succeeding in not making Agatha All Along required viewing. This isn't a show you want to watch without at least having seen WandaVision, but it also does a fine job of explaining everything you need to know about Tommy's bizarre existence without making his brother Billy's (Joe Locke) parallel journey into mandatory homework. It helps the series stand on its own two feet a bit more, rather than simply being the final act of a trilogy.

Another big plus in VisionQuest's favor is that it features such a lovable supporting cast of AI goofballs. James Spader's Ultron doesn't steal the show to quite the degree he did in the first two episodes, but he remains one of the absolute highlights of the series. Ultron is great for both periodic comedic relief and the sorts of knowing observations on human nature that used to be Vision's purview. But we also get to see the character finally take a more purposeful step onto center stage late in Episode 4, as he manipulates his way into taking the wheel (literally) and predictably betrays his family at his first opportunity. The prospect of an Ultron fully in control and back in the physical world is a very exciting one heading into Episode 5.

Speaking of Vision's family, we get a lot of great scenes involving F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), and even D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis) and U (Jonathan Sayer). The series is doing a fantastic job of fleshing out and enriching these characters that used to be nothing more than disembodied voices or slapstick workshop tools. Episode 4 is particularly strong when it comes to exploring their own emotional journeys and how much they parallel what Vision is experiencing.

None of this is to say the series isn't still experiencing some growing pains. Episodes 3 and 4 feel a bit clunky in how they handle the transition from a conflict mostly built around Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to one centered around Jocasta (T'Nia Miller). The former character basically drops out of the picture after running afoul of the latter. Still, I'm enjoying the show's take on Jocasta so far. She's nothing if not sympathetic so far, and she holds a lot of potential as both a villain and the object of Ultron's fascination. All in all, these two episodes do a lot to set up a compelling conflict for the second half of the series.

items.title: Cooking Up Magick Book Review
items.author: Jacob Kienlen
items.content:
: This review contains some minor spoilers for the book.

The first book in a new series called The Dell Chronicles, HL Bernabe’s Cooking Up Magick sets out to be a cozier fantasy version of The Lord of the Rings. And in many ways, it does pull directly from J.R.R. Tolkien’s world. The main character, Paisley, is a halfling who gets swept up on an adventure with a pair of dwarves, but unbeknownst to her, there’s also an evil overlord that has just returned after centuries – and she’s the only hope the world has to actually stop him.

The similarities to The Hobbit and LOTR pretty much end there though, and you don’t get nearly enough detail in the first book to effectively flesh out this alternate version of Middle-earth. What you do get is a lovable main character who is surrounded by an interesting cast of characters. There’s cooking, there’s magic, and there’s even a bit of thrown in here, but Cooking Up Magick doesn’t serve up enough of any of it to fully bring its story to life.

Cooking Up Magick shines brightest whenever the core characters are interacting with each other. Paisley is a bubbly bright spot among the crew, capable of immense courage and compassion. She has a sort of magnetism that rubs off on her friends and which helps shine a light on each of their individual personalities. Her conversations and moments with her newfound friends (and her Half-Orc love interest) really help to ground the story’s core concept of found family.

Naturally, these moments are often centered around the idea of cooking or magic. Paisley’s driving reason for leaving her home and her family’s inn is that she wants to discover new and exciting recipes to eventually bring back. Her sense of adventure is entirely tied to the idea of roaming the world and dipping her toes in the culinary culture it has to offer. But that core motivation quickly fades to the background as larger events start to unfold. There are flashes where cooking comes to the forefront of the story, but it rarely feels like food matters beyond an initial plot driver and a reason for the characters to come together.

"As she learns about her new powers, so do we, and it’s some of the best Paisley character building we get in the entire story

As someone who is always happy to geek out about cooking, I expected the author to showcase more of that in Paisley's character. It’s clear that she likes it, sure, but the writing seems to spend too much time telling us that and not enough time showing it. Going into this book, I had hoped to see Delicious in Dungeon-levels of enthusiasm for cooking and found myself a bit disappointed that it wasn’t what I got.

So while Paisley’s personality doesn’t necessarily shine through her cooking, we do get a better feeling for it through her magical ability. She doesn’t discover her powers until the story progresses a bit, but once they start to manifest, they show up in ways you’d expect from a compassionate chef. She’s able to draw power from her love of her companions and spread that to the world around her. With this power, she’s able to heal, protect, and even connect on a deeper level with her friends. But once she gains her magic, cooking pretty much takes a backseat for the story, and sure, seeing as she’s the first new sorcerer in this world in a really long time, it definitely makes sense for this to take over the story. As she learns about her new powers, so do we, and it’s some of the best Paisley character building we get in the entire story.

Beyond the core characters, much of the book is driven by Verzod, the evil sorcerer. He’s the one who’s inciting war in an otherwise peaceful land, and acts as the obvious antagonist to Paisley (and everyone else). Despite getting multiple chapters from his perspective, it’s hard to draw any other conclusions about him beyond his just being the pure embodiment of evil. The only character depth we’re really able to glean is his soft spot for his lost talking cat, Whipclaw. But since said cat spends most of the book with Paisley, we don’t really get to explore that side of him. I would have much preferred to have left him as a mysterious outside entity that gets revealed in later books, but there’s still plenty of room to flesh out his motives later on. As is, his existence serves its purpose as the inciting action of the story.

items.title: Wicker Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
is in theaters on October 23.

As we’ve learned from stories like Edward Scissorhands, Pinocchio, and Lars and the Real Girl, few things teach us more about what it means to be fully human and alive than creatures crafted by an artist's hands and the desires of one desperate for connection.

A lonely Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) rebels against the limits, forced and chosen, of her lot in life and entreats a Basket Weaver with mystical skills (Peter Dinklage) to craft her a husband made of wicker (Alexander Skarsgård). Despite its unusual premise, Wicker is surprisingly straightforward in its sweetness and condemnation of small cruelties. There are darker elements to the fantasy, including implied violence, visible gore, and the stark reality that frequent death was a fact of this time period, but these ultimately highlight moments of beauty and affirm the need to savor life’s pleasures, be they exultant or sensual. On the whole, the film is warm and charming with real pathos, largely due to the exemplary cast led by Colman, who seemingly effortlessly elevates both the bawdy comedic beats and moments of sorrow and joy. In lesser hands, the humor might have read as pedestrian, and the relationships distant and unrelatable.

Based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones and directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson (Save Yourselves!), Wicker is set in a generic medieval village where all the townspeople are known only by their trade (if male) or their husband’s vocation (if female). The one exception is the Fisherwoman, who has either rejected, or been rejected by, the traditional confines of marriage and as such is known by her profession. The townspeople limit her participation in their world to the periphery, ostensibly due to her potent scent (an occupational hazard). But it’s the Fisherwoman’s refusal to fit into the tightly bound structures their culture demands — which the seaside village’s matriarch, the Tailor’s Wife (Elizabeth Debicki), enforces with an imperious smile — that truly drives her to the edges of their community.

These social constraints feel claustrophobic for everyone, most notably the Fisherwoman, who responds with rebellion, and the Tailor’s Wife, who tries to control others as much as she herself feels confined. That suffocating undercurrent is reinforced by the visual storytelling: The town reads as small and hastily constructed, and the interiors are often dim and candlelit even in daylight, shrouded in mystery (in the Basket Weaver’s workshop) or stifled by the darkness of ignorance (in the villagers’ homes). For the length of the film, we too feel trapped in this deeply flammable village (everything seems to be made of hay or wood!). By contrast, the Fisherwoman’s cottage, set apart from the village, is isolated but surrounded by space, fresh greenery, and a sense of liberation. When the Wicker Husband gets his hands on it, the cottage evolves into something artistically shaped and deeply cared for, a reflection of how he sees his wife; it’s as if the Basket Weaver has passed his artistry on to his creation.

The Wicker Husband himself is stunning, as are all of the Basket Weaver’s designs (even the most ghastly of them), particularly set against the grimier village, where most things and often people are covered in dirt or filth. Weta Workshop built the Wicker Husband with CGI enhancements to appear delicate and precious. When he is damaged, the audience understands that the harm illustrates our own failure to care for something of value. Though eerie, he has the essence of Skarsgård’s natural beauty, and is at once a thing other than human and something more. The actor’s placid tones reflect the character’s innocence, perfectly capturing the Wicker Husband’s ability to point out what isn’t working in the human world simply through his ignorance of it or non-participation in it.

Initially, the Fisherwoman’s purchase of her husband and companion is an act of defiance. She is taunting the villagers, turning their tendency to strip away humanity and objectify themselves and one another on its head. In a reversal of roles, she keeps her title as Fisherwoman while her mate is known simply as the Wicker Husband. This is particularly repellent to the Tailor’s Wife, largely because she longs for the freedom and purpose the Fisherwoman enjoys. In reality, work is both a necessity and a gift for the Fisherwoman, who lacks the privileges of those more embedded in society’s conventions. It gives her meaning but leaves her mostly friendless and often filthy. This exiled, misunderstood woman finds, in the prickly arms of a man made of wood, the acceptance and care missing from much of her village life. The Fisherwoman develops deeper affections for her Wicker Husband than she anticipated and in doing so falls prey to the frailties of real attachment, including jealousy and mistrust, even toward a husband she theoretically “owns” (and who could double as furniture).

Olivia Colman moves from deep vulnerability and self-sabotage to a woman who takes the gift she’s given and runs with it.

The actors ground us in this heightened fable. Early in the film, in a glance of no more than 30 seconds, Colman and Debicki convey the entire shared history of two women who understand, envy, and loathe one another. More saliently, it’s here, with one double take from Colman, that we understand Debicki’s casual mean-spiritedness has sealed the town’s fate: The Fisherwoman will have her say, and with it, a husband the likes of which they cannot imagine — one who will challenge their way of life. Colman brings us into the Fisherwoman’s exuberance as she discovers the nightly joys the Wicker Husband offers, without making it so comical that we’re held at a distance from the character. She delivers a performance that gives the audience catharsis as she moves from deep vulnerability and self-sabotage to a woman who takes the gift she’s given and runs with it.

In a sense, the film asks the viewer to examine how much good we allow ourselves before we damage it, often out of fear that it isn’t real or earned and will therefore betray us. The Fisherwoman, who’s been told she’s not worth much, must wrestle with granting herself permission to feel pleasure (often in spades) and with believing that the sweet can, at the very least, equal the bitter in life. Through witnessing her unorthodox relationship, the whole village is faced with the same inquiry. This is the film’s most interesting idea.

Thematically, Wicker hits at patriarchy with the subtlety of a cudgel. Even in name, the women are reduced to property. The Tailor’s Wife is petty, passive-aggressive, and destructive, in no small part because her natural genius is underused at best and entirely suppressed at worst. We see villagers’ lives imperiled because no one has the will to say that those in charge of critical infrastructure are drunk, incapable, or (often) both. Everyone pays a price for these encrusted traditions. The film is an overt morality play, but with enough surreal humor to keep it from feeling laborious or patronizing.

To its credit, Wicker is seeded with more than just an indictment of utterly ruinous bias. It examines, lightly and with a lot of whimsy, why we all as men and women stay loyal to the restrictions that create pain and discomfort for us, be they social norms or internal limitations. It also asks about the bounds of nature itself, as the Basket Weaver defies the “no” life has given this village's residents. He’ll help them reach for their deepest desires so long as they’re willing to name what they want (whether anyone agrees or not) and care for the small miracles he provides.

It takes a man made of wicker to show this town what it is to be complete and fully human.

Dinklage’s Basket Weaver stands apart from the town but, unlike the Fisherwoman, not in opposition to it. In that sense, he serves as the audience’s surrogate: a somewhat objective observer or Greek chorus who at times goes so far as to monologue or narrate events and who casts the final judgment. Dinklage brings a sense of delight to the role, embodying the Basket Weaver’s love of creating within challenging frameworks, and of doing more than he ever thought himself capable of. He also endows the character with empathy without overplaying his hand. His compassion is reserved chiefly for outsiders like the Fisherwoman, and he disdains the villagers’ inability to extend it to her or even themselves.

It takes a man made of wicker to show this town what it is to be complete and fully human. His way of seeing the world, free of the polluting influence of cultural programming, serves as an (often unwanted) mirror for the villagers, exposing the insanity of mundane life. Ultimately, the film celebrates the rewards of being bold and going for what you want (be that family, vocation, both, or something else altogether) without the need for approval. Though the storytelling in Wicker is fairly direct, Fischer and Wilson have steady hands, and the technical elements combined with the talented cast create an imaginative, immersive, and relatively quick (about an hour and 45 minutes) visit to a universe just to the left of our own, granting us enough distance to see ourselves more clearly.

items.title: We Build LEGO PlayStation, a Near 1:1 Scale Replica of Sony's Classic Console
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
I love LEGO sets based on retro game consoles. They combine two of my favorite things: video games (for obvious reasons) and LEGO sets, with impossibly clever construction mechanics and plenty of Easter eggs.

The latest retro system to become a buildable set is LEGO PlayStation, a near 1:1 scale model of Sony’s original hardware. Now, it may seem like a foregone conclusion today, but the success of the PlayStation was no sure thing when it launched in 1994 in Japan and in 1995 in the US. Many electronics companies had dabbled in the world of video games and failed quickly, with nothing to show for it.

But young me? I was a believer in PlayStation from the start. I remember buying the little gray machine at launch and pouring hundreds of hours into games like Jumping Flash, Battle Arena Toshinden, Street Fighter: The Movie (the game), Twisted Metal, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, Doom, Resident Evil 2, Oddworld: Abe’s Odyssey, Medal of Honor, Metal Gear Solid, Final Fantasy VII through IX (remember when mainline Final Fantasies could come out in a single generation?) and on and on. Man, what an incredible library.

The PS1 provided all the gaming I needed through the latter half of the '90s. I didn’t buy another console until the PlayStation 2 came out after the turn of the millennium.

LEGO PlayStation comes with 1,911 bricks divided into 14 paper bags and takes around six hours to build. Despite the mostly gray exterior, it’s a fun, surprisingly colorful construction from start to finish. It uses a number of clever building techniques along the way, and includes a few delightful Easter eggs.

Even the box for this set is an Easter egg of sorts. It calls back to the box of the original PlayStation.

The process of the build is about what you'd expect: you start by completing the base of the console, and then build your way to the top. But inside of the machine, you first lay down the red, yellow, and blue PS logo, and then build and insert all sorts of colorful little chips and electronic components — many of which you immediately cover up. Unlike the real console, however, you can see some of these "electronics" when you lift the lid.

Also hidden inside the console are two dioramas that slide out on smooth tracks. These are like secret drawers that feature colorful micro-scale worlds for Ape Escape and Gran Turismo, two popular games from the platform. While I didn’t play either of those games back in the day and would have preferred nods to, say, Resident Evil and Metal Gear Solid, they’re still a fun inclusion and I’m sure many fans will appreciate them more than I do.

The set includes one small sheet of stickers. I’ve complained about stickers in LEGO sets before (particularly in LEGO Jurassic Park Jeep Wrangler and LEGO Winnie the Pooh), but they’re more of a minor irritant here. All of the stickers go on the dioramas, which are hidden by default.

All of the most important and visible images on this set — the PlayStation and Sony logos, and the controller’s face button shapes — are pre-printed on the pieces. This is a huge relief for me personally, as I can’t line up a sticker on a LEGO piece perfectly to save my life.

The finished product looks remarkably like a 1:1 representation of the original hardware. If you view it from a distance, you’d be forgiven for thinking it an actual PS1. I dug up my original PlayStation to compare the two devices (I could only find my DualShock controller, not the original). The LEGO set looks incredibly similar to the real thing from almost every angle. The main difference is the LEGO set lacks the RCA ports in the back, which isn’t a big deal (see the slideshow below for more comparison pics).

Even the Power and Open buttons on the finished set “work.” Pressing Power lifts a little green translucent rod into view, right where the green power light is on the original hardware. Pressing the Open button releases a latch that, thanks to a spring-loaded mechanism, raises the disc lid, just like it does on the original.

I have a few minor complaints about LEGO PlayStation. My Open button sticks when I press it all the way in, so the lid won’t close unless I fiddle with the button to make it pop back out. The controller also looks a little janky, but I understand it’s hard or impossible to make an exact replica LEGO version of something so curvy.

If you’re a gamer of a certain age and have fond memories of playing then-newfangled CD-based games on an original PlayStation, I can wholeheartedly recommend this set. It would also make a fine gift, if someone you know falls into that category.

items.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Back in 2022, Nintendo attempted to revive the fun and charm of the motion-controlled Wii Sports era, but it didn’t quite live up to that lofty goal. Now in 2026, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort takes another swing at that same difficult feat with a clear focus on “more.” More sports, more outfits, more modes, and more collectibles. That doesn't always translate to a better package, with Sports Resort often feeling a wide ocean rather than a deep diving pool, but it more than makes up for it with a broad range of games ripe to bust out at the next big party. So while it may not clear the high bar set by the original Wii Sports in 2006, it still brings out the same child-like joy.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a collection of 12 different sports minigames, ranging from highly competitive one-on-one Table Tennis to leisurely cruising in a prop plane around Wuhu Island where they all take place. The quality of each game varies drastically. Archery is a standout thanks to its unique use of the Joy-Con controllers, while a returning sport like Basketball is largely untouched and still feels too choreographed – it's once again missing the freedom of movement and control I want so desperately from a potential party version.

The new sports can also be hit and miss. Power Cruising uses two Joy-Con held like you are gipping handlebars to simulate racing a jet ski, but those clunky controls don’t always work well, so it feels more like a gimmick rather than a fun sport. On the other hand (quite literally),Thumb Wrestling helps bring whimsy to the package. It’s extremely silly, but actually makes for some competitive matches – in my online sessions, I was pleasantly surprised with how strategy and tactics changed from match to match. Watching players develop new ways to trick and bait their opponents into getting caught in their trap was entertaining, and I found myself determined to never let anyone get the best of me.

Archery is easily the best sport offered in Sports Resort. With four different courses scattered around Wuhu Island, it feels the most well-thought out. I stretched out my arms in front of me, holding both Joy-Con perpendicular to the floor, then clicked the ZL button with my left hand and drew it back to my chest like I would draw a real bow. Using my right Joy-Con to aim at a distant target, it was satisfying every time I hit my mark. More challenging courses and hidden targets to find help flesh out Archery overall, which meant it provided hours of fun for my friends and I in a way many of the thinner options don’t.

As you might expect, playing through Sports Resort by myself proved to be a bit lackluster, as it lacks the competitive spirit so intrinsic to the games it recreates. Island Crown, a new mode that has you climb the ranks in nine of the 12 sports, pushed me forward with a little bit of structure and challenge, but even then I found my enthusiasm waning before too long.

Its loose story has you defeat challengers in order to eventually face the island champion, who – depending on the sport – will either taunt or cheer you on after every victory. Upon defeating one of the island champions you'll unlock a few more extra objectives in the given sport. Sometimes it's an Island Legend looking for a fight, others it’s a gauntlet of challengers that need to be defeated without losing. It's a decent distraction for those looking to casually play sports while your friends and family aren't around to party, and that’s about it.

But when they are around, Sports Resort is easily the game I want to break out. So much of the joy of these games is heightened when folks in the room are cheering, yelling, and getting so into it you need to remind everyone to keep the Joy-Con wrist strap on. This has always been the spirit of the Nintendo Sports games, and Sports Resort is one of the best versions of it around when you've got the crew to play.

Recruiting my roommates to run through the sports on a Sunday afternoon was an eye-opening experience. Games like Volleyball – which I found to be incredibly boring during my time with Island Crown and casual single-player – became electric back and forth rallies that lit up the room. Exhausted cheers, disappointing sighs, and questionable calls made even some of the more mundane sports like Golf feel exhilarating.And quick, snappy menus make hopping between sports seamless as well, which kept everyone from zoning out between rounds.

Even leisure sports like Skateboarding quickly became heated competitions as we slammed our Joy-Con on the table in mouse mode, ready to race. Skateboarding is the only game in Sports Resort that takes advantage of this control scheme, effectively turning the Joy-Con into a mini Tech Deck. Intuitive controls like flicking your hand to the left or right did 360 pop shuv-its and quickly lifting the front it off the table produced an ollie. With multiple race courses, we ripped through each one attempting to best one another, constantly pushing for faster times as our rivalry grew.

My only real complaint about the local multiplayer is that games like Boxing require participants to have two Joy-Con each, meaning you aren't able to play those sports at all if you only have the single pair that came with the Switch 2. So if you're planning on having folks over to box , ask them to bring some extra controllers.

It turns out that while Power Cruising requires the use of two Joy-Con while playing single-player, there is an option to use just one per person in multiplayer. Additionally, older Joy-Con from the original Switch can be used for any sport except Skateboarding. The previous paragraph has been ammended and we apologize for the error.]

When we needed to cool down, we hopped into the Sightseeing Tour mode, which allows you to zoom around Wuhu Island in search of points of interest marked with giant floating cameras. Collecting a camera marks it on your Sightseeing Log and gives you a little flavor about that part of the island. It's a neat way to get a sense of how all of the sports fit together contextually in this space, and allows you to visit other islanders while they compete on the tennis courts, archery ranges, and more.

Between Archery rounds or Thumb Wrestling matches, I would routinely hop into my Prop Plane to fly around the island in search of more Sightseeing Logs. The five-minute timer makes it an excellent bit sized adventure that rewards you for exploring a different part of the island on each outing. Going off the beaten path proved fruitful every time, with plenty of secrets to find for those willing to be curious.

It would be really easy for Sports Resort to be nothing more than a series of menus as you bounce between sports, with no connective throughline to follow. Sightseeing Tour gives everything a sense of place, and strengthens the quirkiness found on the outskirts of it all. Blimps fly high in the sky, speedboats race into the distance, and plenty of characters can be found hanging in parts of the island you would never see by just playing the basic sports. Leisure sports also offer a free roam mode which allows you to explore to your hearts content.

That said, sports like Tennis, Basketball, Thumb Wrestling, and a few others have just one set location each, which does get old. I wish there was more variety in where they could be played across Wuhu Island, because it became unexciting to see the same background for my 30th Thumb Wrestling match – even if the Mii's in the background were different from the match before.

If your friends are farther away, Sports Resort has online play with both casual and pro-league options. Casual uses a lobby system that allows multiple people to party up and play games together. If a two-player game is selected, you can even form multiple huddles in the same lobby, playing separate sports at the same time. However, there is no way to spectate someone else's game, which is a bit of a let down. I would love to be able to watch friends play Tennis or take out their aggression in a Thumb Wrestling match.

Each sport also has special modes that change up the gameplay just enough to be fresh for a bit, but I didn't find any of them exciting enough to return to time and time again. Bowling adds its classic obstacles to the lane, which require more creative strategies and fancy footwork to overcome, while Archery has four people compete for points on the same target, attempting to avoid an opponent's section as you hit your own. These modes are a fun break, but don't go much further beyond that.

Everything you do in Sports Resort also nets your Spocco Points, which can be spent at a rotating shop. The shop sells themed items in a set, and 1,000 Spocco will get you one item randomly pulled from that set. You won't receive duplicates, but it is strange that you can't just choose the items you want. Being forced into a random roll feels like it just artificially inflates the amount of Spocco needed to get what you want.

The customization is rather robust at least, with no shortage of fancy outfits, namecard titles, face paints, and so much more – you’ll unlock bevy of different options by playing Island Crown as well, ranging from leather studded gloves for Thumb Wrestling to unique volleyball attire. I was constantly gaining Spocco, and while it was a little tiresome to be frequently reminded to check out the shop as I earned points for miscellaneous things like shaking the Joy-Con 1,000 times, at least the rewards for doing so were neat.

items.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Review
items.author: jon Burgess
items.content:
To evoke the classics is also to hold yourself to the high standard set by them. With Final Fantasy Resonance bringing the venerated series back to its origins with turn-based combat, and wielding Square’s HD-2D art style to modernize nostalgia for the pixel art era, it plucks at something I've longed for as someone who grew up in the SNES generation. While I've expressed my love for the Octopath Traveler series time and again, Final Fantasy has of course crystalized into something meaningful over the past several decades. But as much as Resonance looks like a torchbearer for classic RPGs, it also goes for a style of storytelling that often rings hollow. So, I think of it as a game of moments – when a genre-fusing boss theme graces your ears, when you execute a turn perfectly and watch all your spells fire off with big damage numbers, and when a cutscene brings HD-2D to life in a way you've just never seen before.

Resonance adapts the story and characters from the now-shuttered mobile game Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius by packaging them into the structure of a traditional RPG; no gacha mechanics, no microtransactions. It's quite similar to what Square Enix did with Octopath Traveler 0 and it's a brilliant way to bring existing stories into a format I'm a lot more inclined to play. With that comes an overworld with towns to represent each region, random encounters, an airship for roaming free and discovering pieces of land that feel like secrets, and full voice acting throughout the main story.

It largely sticks to the events of the first season of Brave Exvius, which follows the knights from the Kingdom of Grandshelt, Rain and Laswell, the mysterious magical girl born from a crystal, Fina, along with additional friends on a quest to stop the armor-clad Sworn Six from destroying the world's crystals and plunging it into calamity. Of course, there's more beneath the surface. That said, a lot of dialogue and interstitial events have been added to fill out the journey, which took me about 45 hours to complete (including all of the side quests marked on my map and poking around the overworld for optional minibosses who offer intense challenges). While chunks of Resonance's story aren't very riveting, the production value here had me forgetting that this was built on the bones of a mobile game – not that Brave Exvius was any lesser of an achievement for what it was.

That retooling extends to gameplay, which retains concepts and mechanics that work extremely well as an engaging turn-based combat system – and hearing "turn-based" and Final Fantasy in the same breath after all these years released those good chemicals in my brain, too. This is not an ATB system with an active element, but a straightforward turn order along a timeline. And the way you either plan accordingly depending on which units are up or manipulate the order to your advantage had me employing similar strategies as I do in the Trails series or the Octopath Traveler games.

It's all about elemental affinities and staggering enemies in Resonance, however. Each party member has their own set of elements covered through magic spells or element-imbued physical attacks, but they also equip what are called Visions that function somewhat like a Job system directly inspired by Final Fantasy V. This is what provides flexibility in party composition, giving you the tools to make sure you either cover all the elements or go all-in on a specific type so you can streamroll bosses. While every attack chips at an enemy's stagger meter, hitting their weaknesses is, of course, the strategy demanded of you.

I'm of two minds with this system: while it’s nice to have flexibility as you swap Visions between party members to constantly change their overall movesets, it can sometimes trivialize your combat approach. For example, going into a water-themed boss fight, I knew purely electric builds were going to be the optimal strategy.
