So, while it was rad as hell to watch chunks of stagger and HP get chopped off as I spammed electric attacks, I often didn't feel the need to think much harder than that. Having the foresight to anticipate the right element before a fight isn't quite as rewarding as being pushed to scheme with what you have.

HD-2D animations look so good and hit with emphatic impact.

Compare this to the boost and break system of an Octopath Traveler, where the tools you're given are more dynamic and free-flowing even with elemental affinities involved, which then lets you get more creative rather than just having you hammer away with one specific element. I cruised through the first half of Resonance since most enemies and bosses were pushovers. But thankfully, things got tougher in the late game where they hit harder and inflicted more status ailments to work around. Key moments where I was challenged to think steps ahead culminated in some real hard-fought battles toward the end.

Overall, it still provides enough of the puzzle-esque tactical thinking that's required of a good turn-based RPG. Party members level up alongside their mastery of equipped Visions, but you have to manually rank up Visions then apply passive perks and support spells, which gets into some interesting buildcrafting that gives a little extra depth that mattered for those big fights. And I enjoyed Resonance's combat system because it still captures the satisfaction of teeing off on a staggered enemy with your nastiest spells, especially because their animations look so good and hit with emphatic impact.

Visions themselves are super fun to toy with because most of them are avatars of star characters from Final Fantasy's past. Their movesets call back to specific spells and signature attacks from their respective games, and it's nice to see parts of the series' history celebrated in a way that's integral to how Resonance plays. Staggering an enemy grants extra turns in a bonus phase, and staggering all of them (or a lone foe) leads to the sweeping stagger phase where everyone gets to pile on, which then concludes in a Resonance attack tied to a Vision of your choosing. I still find it jarring to go from beautiful HD-2D to a CGI cutscene (pulled from Brave Exvius) when summoning a Resonance attack, some of these are pretty cool, like big Shanttoto throwing a massive boulder of dark energy or Clive getting ready to hit L3+R3 to accept the truth. There's some wonderful pixel art around those cuts that look incredible, too, like Lightning, who gets a full animation set here – and it's lovely to see these characters recreated in that style.

Each is obtained by visiting shrines sprinkled throughout the overworld and going through a quiz-like dialogue sequence that walks through the events of their own stories (and beware, there are some major spoilers for Final Fantasies you have not played yet). I found this pretty cheesy at first, but it really grew on me as a reminder of how each entry captured something powerful that has stood the test of time. You never really know which shrine belongs to who, so when their music kicks in, it had me grinning ear-to-ear – and as someone who was deeply touched by FFXIV Shadowbringers, hearing "Tomorrow and Tomorrow" and recounting Y'shtola's ongoing story is a prime example of how sometimes Resonance me.

More than the hard-fought battles against god-like beings, Final Fantasy has stuck around and won our hearts because of the stories it tells. And this is where I wrestled most with Resonance. The foundations of its story are quite solid and consistent as a classic Final Fantasy about the power of crystals that fuel these magical worlds and defeating evil to save the world against villains who reveal themselves to be more complicated by story's end. But it's always about those stories get told and the impactful themes they explore along the way. Resonance has glimpses of hitting those same highs, yet I found long stretches of its storytelling to be quite underwhelming.

Taking the story of Brave Exvius and expanding on it was definitely worth exploring, but Resonance fills out a lot of that time with dialogue that feels like it was written for a middling young adult novel then crammed into a fantasy world. Not that fantasy stories to be Shakespearean or high-concept, but much of Resonance reads like a script that didn't get punched up; overly talkative where it takes five lines for something that could've been said in one, and banking on a contemporary twee tone and some mustache-twirly villains. I love melodrama, long cutscenes, and tropes like the power of friendship, and Resonance has that for sure, but doesn't start dialing it in until late in the game.

But there's still something enticing about going on a journey with characters who overcome unbelievable odds. I came around on lead protagonist Rain and his brother-in-arms Lasswell because, while simple characters, they have a bond that riled me up for the conclusion. Fina turns out to be a little bit more than someone with a mysterious, dark past and was a compelling way to weave in more of the magical storytelling devices sensibly. The stern tactician Nichol and pink-haired mage Sakura turn out to be the better written characters who fit the RPG mold so well; and the emotional arc Nichol goes through is genuine and one of the few ways the story shows some depth. However, I struggled to care about the Sworn Six since a lot of their dialogue undersells their importance to the broader lore. And that Dr. Lazarov is an incredibly annoying throwaway who is nothing more than a mad scientist to roll your eyes at.

Resonance also struggles with narrative momentum because it's shrouded in a vagueness that blurs its throughline rather than luring you in. So, it relies more on the societal issues of each region – environmental tragedies, revolt against a tyrannical government, or underclasses being exploited. These stories are delivered decently on their own, but the thematic coherence didn't come until much later, and how it all tied together through the mysterious ways of magic was predictable, if not fine.

Sometimes music resonates more powerfully than words, and it's one of the things I'll remember most.

Now, it usually takes more than spectacle to win me over, but Final Fantasy Resonance is an exception. When it matters most, the strongest moments are uplifted with some of the best cutscene work in HD-2D, wielding camera movement in a 3D plane effectively as character sprites and pixelized special effects coalescence through fluid animation that conveys emotion dialogue wouldn't be able to capture alone. The art style may have been born out of nostalgia, but Resonance proves that we're past that point and it can lead to new, evocative ways of creating worlds and elevating stories beyond the sum of their parts.

Music also plays a large role in why I look back at my time with Resonance fondly. It may be the expectation for a Final Fantasy game to have an amazing soundtrack, but the way certain town themes employ instruments that instill the feeling of a brutal, industrialized empire or a mystical city floating in the sky is magical. From the normal battle theme to the different tiers of bosses, I realized that Brave Exvius' great soundtrack was here all along and played off of many of the musical themes attached to the series. Remixing a dungeon theme into a bouncy electronic tune was like having fire come out of my headphones. And my jaw dropped when I heard a boss theme remix that had piano jazz fused with orchestral metal, a double bass drum pedal, and a latin choir that in a way that came together in unexpected harmony; it's such an impressive song I still can't get out of my head. Sometimes music resonates more powerfully than words, and it's one of the things I'll remember most.

items.title: Capturing Bigfoot Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
is playing in select theaters and is available to rent or buy on Prime Video starting October 20.

Bigfoot is alive and was born in Yakima, Washington.

Keep your hairy suits on; the mythical creature is not in the same way you and I are. However, he remains alive in the public imagination. One of the primary reasons for this, as seen in director Marq Evans’ fascinating documentary Capturing Bigfoot, has to do with a short film made way back in 1967 by a group of Washingtonians that supposedly captured footage of the creature walking with a memorably lumbering gait in the remote woods of California. The infamous Patterson-Gimlin film, named for two of its creators, Roger Patterson (who died in 1972) and Robert “Bob” Gimlin, has continued to endure over the decades, picked apart by doubters just as it is still held up as almost a sacred document by believers.

It’s a subject that’s ripe for deeper analysis, and Capturing Bigfoot – which premiered back at this year’s SXSW Film & TV Festival, where it already began to make waves in the Bigfoot community – not only delivers on that front, but also in its look at the people who made the 1967 film. It’s a solidly entertaining watch, bringing to light the reality of what's out there lurking in the woods, but it also offers something more in how it gets at the deeper, more painful, and yet still beautiful psychological mysteries living inside the human mind.

While Evans gives plenty of attention to the Bigfoot of it all and the hold it has over so many, critically, he’s not making a film that’s solely about the creature. Instead, that is, if anything, merely the entry point to something far more illuminating. With patient, incisive filmmaking and thoughtful care, Evans uncovers not only the truth about the Patterson-Gimlin film – and the being it “captured” – but also infinitely more valuable revelations about the people who made it and those who now have to live with its legacy. While this all builds to a genuinely stunning revelation by showing what is essentially the most significant “deleted scene” in Bigfoot cinema history, it's the journey of getting there that makes Capturing Bigfoot a consistently compelling gem. You come to see all of not only who Roger Patterson was, but the impact his film had on his son, Clint, as he sorts through his father’s legacy. Is Roger a trickster who lied to his son and everyone he knew? Is he a filmmaker in his own right who made an enduring work of cinema? Or is he just another struggling hustler who was trying to carve out his piece of the ever-elusive American dream?

There is a compassion to the filmmaking, even as the subjects are made to confront the lies that surround them and have shaped their lives.

Ultimately, the Patterson patriarch was trying to tell a story that, yes, he could use to make some money, but it became much more than that. To both those who knew him and many who didn’t, his film became something that provided so much over the years. We hear this not just from Clint, but also those like the late Bigfoot expert (and academic) Jeffrey Meldrum, who attended a screening of the film as a child shortly after it was made. The experience left an impact on Meldrum and gave him something to believe in as an adult, so to then hear it may have all been premised on a lie is a psychologically difficult thing to reckon with. As Meldrum says at one point, sounding more than a little anxious, he feels like he’s being led “up to a precipice and you’re just about to push me over the edge.” When he later watches new footage that upends everything that he’d come to believe about Bigfoot, we see in his eyes that so much of his worldview and life’s purpose is crumbling.

Even as this could all seem rather silly or, even worse, cruel or exploitative, Evans never looks down on his subjects or seeks to take advantage of them. There is a compassion to the filmmaking, even as the subjects are made to confront the lies that surround them and have shaped their lives. Evans asks the tough questions when he needs to and doesn’t shy away from the more thorny reality of what actually happened, but he also works to understand what it was about the film and Bigfoot that still means so much to many of those he talks to.

Whether the Patterson-Gimlin film is a fake or not, it’s not going to stop people from believing in Bigfoot or anything else that they need to. It’s not about what makes factual sense, but what makes emotional sense and allows such folks to feel like they have some agency over the stories in their lives. There is a painfully tragic dimension to this, as such ideas are inherently built upon buying into a delusion, but it’s also a deeply human, occasionally darkly humorous, and potentially dangerous reality of our world. Even as Capturing Bigfoot doesn’t fully dive into the more expansive implications of this, it does reveal the darker truths and lies that can exist within all of us. There will always be the things we build our lives around and hold closely to. This one just happened to take the form of a giant, hairy cryptid. Thus, while the physical being may not be real, there will always be more Bigfoots. Bigfoot is dead. Long live Bigfoot.

items.title: Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Cyberpunk: Edgerunners felt like a revelation. Like Castlevania and Arcane before it, the series delivered a stunning video game adaptation that told an original story with memorable characters rather than trying to forcefully redo the game’s storyline, all while still very much feeling like a part of its source material’s world. Add in a phenomenal soundtrack and Hiroyuki Imaishi’s striking visual flare, and you have one of the best sci-fi animé series of all time.

Now we’re back in Night City for a new standalone sequel in the larger Cyberpunk universe, though Edgerunners 2 does tie into the story of David Martinez from the first 10-episode series in key ways while also connecting to the main story of Cyberpunk 2077. No, you don’t need to have experienced either to enjoy this new story, but it does pay off to know more about the world of Night City.

From the get-go, Edgerunners 2 tries to do things differently than its predecessor. Rather than focusing on one character experiencing the horrors of Night City, we follow multiple characters and storylines. We mostly see the action through the eyes of two of them: The first is Weak Kingsley, an edgerunner who survives going cyberpsycho early on and has his chrome downgraded (again, this makes more sense if you know the world). Aimless and struggling to adjust to his new reality, Kingsley gets involved in the story when he’s asked by an old flame to rescue a young girl named Talia from the Maelstrom — a cult obsessed with body modifications and leaving their humanity behind. Then we have Roman Carax, a 12-year-old kid and amateur filmmaker with a disdain for the crudeness of braindances (watching someone’s memories from their point-of-view) and an obsession with old-school cinema and analog filmmaking. Roman gets involved when he takes a job making a video of the Maelstrom in exchange for a 35mm camera.

Roman spending the entire series documenting the action with his camera gives Edgerunners 2 a ’90s anime feel, often appearing moody and gritty to match the darkness and violence of the story. Director Kai Ikarashi keeps the expressionistic aesthetic, bright colors, and sharp angles of the first series while adding his own flair to this follow-up. Particularly striking is the constant change of art style, both to reflect the psyche of certain characters or to show how technology impacts how they view the world. There’s a penchant for minimalistic visuals, highlighting shadows and silhouettes, that makes this sequel stand out from the already dazzling first series and creates an aesthetic of its own.

Edgerunners 2 also trades the class warfare themes of the first series — with its indictment of Night City’s hyper-capitalism and its tragic underdog story of desperate people — for a story about corporations purposely messing with people’s lives for their own gain and even working with gangs to destroy communities. It’s a different approach for sure, with the sequel series favoring plotting and world-building over the more emotional and intimate story of the first series. Unfortunately, it means the big picture takes a while to become clear and the many storylines can feel convoluted and sprawling at first. The characters come across as less relatable and fleshed out, since a big part of their development is treated as a mystery to be slowly unraveled. That being said, we still meet a memorable group of poor, unfortunate souls trying to survive in the hell that is Night City.

It can still be surprising to see how Studio Trigger comes up with new ways to make bodies explode on screen without feeling repetitive.

Even if their individual character arcs aren’t out of this world, the way they play into the overall plot of the season is thrilling to see. This is especially true of the way the season works in the story of the Relic and Soulkiller from Cyberpunk 2077. It serves to greatly expand the world of Edgerunners, making it feel like the story we’re following in the episodes is but a small chapter in a much larger saga of the city. When the storylines finally merge, it’s quite satisfying to see the larger picture come alive as the action gets bigger and takes on a bit of an Akira inspiration, with full-on body horror on display. It’s no surprise that the violence is a highlight of Edgerunners 2, but it can still be surprising to see how Studio Trigger comes up with new ways to make bodies explode on screen without feeling repetitive.

items.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Review So Far
items.author: Simon Cardy
items.content:
This review covers Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign and traditional multiplayer PvP modes. It will be updated with a final score early next week, and you can find our standalone

Another year, another Call of Duty. This time it’s developer Infinity Ward’s turn to deliver the next chapter in its Modern Warfare saga, and it does so impressively in an all-action campaign full of twists and turns. Moments of consequence are aplenty in a particularly dark tale of personal vendettas and explosive invasions, played out across a set of missions that largely hit the mark. The single-player shines, then, but the multiplayer portion of Modern Warfare 4 is quite a bit duller. Solid foundations and a novel new arena ensure there’s plenty of fun to be had, but the majority of its new modes and maps do little to excite due to some unimaginative design choices and awkward spawn positions. The combination of these two halves is a much-needed reminder of what Call of Duty be at its best, even if it can’t fully recapture the heights of its glory days.

Modern Warfare 4 Campaign

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign has been set an unenviable task: tie the bow on a seven-year-long series of stories I’d politely describe as “uneven.” To its credit, it handles this challenge well, delivering a genuinely exciting string of missions that are great when they focus on what is new, rather than getting bogged down in the past. It’s the best Modern Warfare has been since its 2019 reboot by quite some distance, and a reminder of how good Call of Duty can be when the people making it are given time to cook.

This collection of blockbuster sequences that has clearly been built from the ground up as a single-player experience is in stark contrast when compared to 2023’s woeful Modern Warfare 3 campaign, arguably the low point of the entire series. A mishmash of multiplayer maps mixed with slivers of near-incomprehensible story, I don’t envy Infinity Ward having to pick up from where it left off. The studio has done about as good a job as it could, though, thanks to a smart structure which splits the two halves of this story until they inevitably collide, providing both variety in mission design and tone.

Captain Price has been at the centre of the Modern Warfare plot, and that doesn’t change too much here. Following the disastrous finale of Modern Warfare 3, he’s now on the run, acting as a lone wolf, wanted by the very people he used to work for. His half of the story is initially tied up in knots so twisted even Alfred Borden would have trouble with them. Infinity Ward’s answer? Take a machete to much of it and kill off any characters introduced in the past two games that it deems superfluous. It’s almost an admission of guilt over how poorly these people were handled in the past, but it does give a sense of finality to this seemingly saga-ending chapter.

A tale of string-pullers and warmongers, Price’s story takes place over the course of five days in the run-up to the North Korean invasion of South Korea (plenty more on that in a moment). The former SAS captain has the blinkers on for his nemesis Makarov and whoever his boss may be. It’s fair to say that the Russian terrorist is not close to being the well-developed threat from the original Modern Warfare 2, which feels like a wasted opportunity to revive a famous villain. In his place steps Mads Mikkelsen’s The Archer.

For the most part, Price’s chapters of the story play like a Bond movie, packed full of parkour escapes, car chases, and stealthy infiltrations. Mikkelsen’s casting only reinforces this feeling, and while he’s classically unsettling in his performance, his character was never given quite enough screen time for me to grow a connection with him. As such, while the missions that make up Price’s side of the story are fun, it comes across as the weaker half. Infinity Ward clearly wants Price to be the strongest emotional bond to the player and for his personal vendettas to feel like our own, but, in truth, many more of the missions are dedicated to the Korean conflict. Incidentally, this is also where I found a lot more of the engaging storytelling to be found.

Modern Warfare 4’s 16 missions took me around the world as well as back and forth in time. The Korean invasion takes place in the “present day” as I followed a squad of soldiers from the moment war is sparked to its conclusion, while we switch back to Price every now and then as he hunts for whoever is behind the plot in the preceding week. These time shifts also allow for a clever mixture between traditional military missions and behind-enemy-lines ingenuity. For example, an early level has you fistfighting and gun-fu-ing your way through a New York nightclub as Price puts on his best John Wick impression. The next, you’ll be holding off paratroopers on the streets of Seoul armed with a mortar. While the Korean sections are generally louder and more traditional boots-on-the-ground “Call of Duty” in their approach, it came somewhat as a surprise to me that it managed to build such a strong connection to its playable character.

Stranded embraces freedom of approach as few other missions do.

There’s an endearing nature to Young Mazino's Park Hyun Jun. Just as Farah did in 2019’s reboot, he gives an emotional anchor to the story that offsets the gruff military types nicely. The same can be said for his whole squad, a mixture of Korean and US soldiers who maintain a well-balanced mixture of levity and seriousness. Their bonds rooted me in its events well, and I actually cared what happened to them by the end. In general, I found the Korean side of things much more compelling and ended up caring about the likes of Park, his friend Jae, and their northern counterpart, Ko, a lot more. While Mikkelsen’s The Archer can come across as a moustache-twirling, nuclear weapon-wielding caricature at times, Modern Warfare 4 actually does a good job of bringing depth to the North Korean threat instead of painting each and every one of its leaders and people following their orders in one shade of evil.

The general direction of the story may not surprise you, but there are some engaging character moments that the past couple of Modern Warfare installments have desperately lacked. One such moment happens during one of the campaign’s standout missions: Stranded. As is the way these days, Call of Duty is now an interconnected beast, so this particular mission actually gives you a taste of Modern Warfare 4’s DMZ extraction mode as it takes you deep behind enemy lines. Due to your stranded nature, you have to go out into the wild and forage for ways to rebuild your arsenal by raiding outposts or heading to mystery markers on the map, then head back to the safety of your basement hideout to craft new equipment. What could so easily come across as a glorified, crowbarred tutorial does actually fit in and play around with the larger story in interesting ways.

Tasked with three main objectives to complete in any order you choose across a large snowy map, Stranded embraces freedom of approach as few other missions do. You could fast travel between the three key locations and move on with the story quickly if you’d like, or spend a couple of hours unlocking each of its snow-covered secrets, ranging from exotic weaponry to keypad-based puzzles to solve. It’s an evolution of Black Ops 6’s Phantom Pain-inspired open zone mission, trading in the sand for a much cooler climate that I enjoyed skulking around with my thermal-scoped sniper rifle. It’s elegantly folded into the campaign, too, making each of its chosen mechanics make narrative sense while also being very fun to play through.

This expansive chapter was the standout mission across the roughly seven hours it took me to complete the campaign, alongside Korea’s answer to D-Day – opening with a beach landing from hell where Infinity Ward’s phenomenal sound design gets to shine – and an airfield escape in which you can dynamically switch characters at will to hold off your attackers. The latter contains a great sense of spectacle that felt like pure Call of Duty at its core. These huge-scale operations are often the highlight, with the amount of moving parts at times simply astonishing. It’s a full-blown campaign crafted to be played like one, not a hodgepodge of other modes where the story feels held together with sticky tape. A sweet relief when compared to what preceded it three years prior. That being said, while the quality of the missions is consistently very good, there isn’t a genuine all-timer here to rival the likes of All Ghillied Up or Clean House, either.

That consistency only stumbles once or twice, usually when forcing you into some unforgiving stealth segments or asking you to engage in its imprecise counter-based melee system. First-person thumping can be disorienting at the best of times, and it's not done particularly well here. This is made even more frustrating by the fact that it often rears its head during some of the story’s key moments, meaning having to retry these brawls lessens the impact of what should feel like emotional hammer blows. Rest assured, these are rare occasions, though. For the most part, I enjoyed the mixture of new ideas being blended with age-old Call of Duty staples. Chopper gunner raids, night vision ambushes, and explosive tank sections. They all still hit the mark. Especially when soundtracked by some fantastically emphatic music at times — the Korean battles in particular are scored with some adrenaline-fuelled electronic orchestrations.

The gunplay is refined, packing the sort of punch we’ve come to expect from Infinity Ward, but still shouldn’t be taken for granted. Movement is slick, being able to transition from a sprint into a slide, before mounting onto a pillar and peeking around the corner to pop a head peeking out of cover. No, enemy AI may not be the smartest, but that doesn’t mean you should play them for fools. Even on regular difficulty, get a little cocky and opt for the run-and-gun approach and your health bar won’t last too long. Managing your ammo, armour plates, and cover is needed, especially towards the campaign’s latter missions. Enemy variety may be limited, but a few heavily armoured brutes caused me quite a bit of trouble when trying to stay out of the blast of their shotguns in some tight underground tunnels. Nothing a few stolen explosive shells of my own couldn’t eventually sort out, though.

Modern Warfare 4 Multiplayer

There’s always a slight adjustment period when switching from Black Ops to Modern Warfare multiplayer. After two years with BLOPS, I trained my brain to expect a longer time to kill when playing Call of Duty, while Modern Warfare is traditionally the faster shooter by comparison. It's somewhat surprising, then, that Modern Warfare 4 actually feels slower than either Black Ops 6 or 7, but I'm by no means against this. That longer time to kill and a few extra bullets needed to defeat an enemy (or deplete your own health bar) lead to more thoughtful encounters. I've enjoyed being able to dip in and out of duels rather than it feeling like whoever spotted the other person first automatically wins.

A similar thing can be said for movement, which is pleasingly simple. There's no tac sprint, omnimovement, or wall-running to worry about this time, which I find a real blessing. Yes, some of these abilities could result in impressive John Woo moments, but more often they got frustrating in the heat of the action as half of the enemy team flew about the place in a slapstick manner. I appreciate Modern Warfare 4's commitment to placing its excellent gunplay front and center instead. Each gun feels great to wield, with assault rifles once again often coming out as my primary weapon of choice, with the occasional foray into SMGs and shotguns for some of Modern Warfare 4’s smaller maps.

Speaking of maps, there’s one new star of the show: Kill Block. An advanced, scenery-shifting military training facility, its unique quirk is that each time you play it, things will be different. The arena is split up into three sections, each randomised at the beginning of every other round of Gunfight — the tense, one-life-only team-based mode that has been a personal favourite ever since its 2019 introduction. For example, the match could begin with a smattering of shipping containers in the middle third of the map, only for that to change to the helicopter wreckage of the classic COD map, Crash, just minutes later. It’s a smart way to both keep each battle fresh and weave nostalgia and familiarity into its randomness. Plus, the way each component’s selection is presented as some sort of one-armed bandit of war spinning into position is good fun, too.

For now, only Gunfight is playable on Kill Block, in a fantastic 10v10 version, which gloriously mixes in early round chaos with nail-biting tension as the seconds tick down and only a few players remain. Over time, the more traditional multiplayer modes such as Team Deathmatch and Kill Confirmed will be added to the mix, though, and I can see the map becoming a real fan favourite by the end of Modern Warfare 4’s year-long cycle.

That’s good news, because I can’t say that the rest of the 12 maps included at launch grabbed my attention in anywhere near the same way. The tight streets of Mumbai can lead to some fun fights by offering a clear and easily readable three-lane structure, but Cachette’s central courtyard is a deathtrap surrounded by high windows that make it a nightmare to run through. Then there are the ones that elicit zero emotion from me at all, such as the rather nondescript snow of Sentry and industrial brown factory of Coal, neither of which have got me rushing back for more just yet.

Most of these maps suffer from what feel like significant spawning issues at this early stage, too. There’s no real pattern to where you start off after dying. Often I feel like I’m dumped into a corner of one that’s nowhere near any of my teammates and left to fend for myself, or sometimes right into the line of fire of an enemy. It can lead to a fairly miserable time if you get caught in one of these loops when several respawns in a row leave you up against it.

I would have liked to see more of the same innovation Kill Block showed.

It’s always a challenge each year for Call of Duty’s developers to introduce new maps to the mix when so many classic crowd pleasers already exist, so it's a credit to Infinity Ward that Kill Block already feels like it could be heading in that direction, but I would have liked to see a bit more of that same innovation. I already have one eye on that incoming Shipment 24/7 mode just days away, craving some of that tight-quarters mayhem which never grows old. I’m glad it's here, but it doesn’t necessarily show a great sense of confidence in the launch set of maps.

One thing you’ll struggle to complain about is the sheer amount of stuff packed into this game. Just in multiplayer alone, there are many, modes to pick from, ranging from core staples to riffs on other online first-person shooters. One of those is Collateral, a Search and Destroy-esque plant and defuse mode that pits attackers against defenders over the course of several rounds, with added buy stages like Counter-Strike or Valorant. It sometimes manages to capture the suspense that those other games thrive on, but lacks the tactical edge that makes them special. When the objective is prioritised, I enjoyed myself, but too often it devolves into a 5v5 version of Gunfight where the bomb is largely ignored in favour of just killing the other team. Call of Duty players (myself included) have never been objective-minded, so this isn’t a huge surprise, but it does hamstring the mode quite a bit.

Where I could at least find some fun in Collateral, I can’t say the same thing about Frontline — a spawn-kill hellscape. Basically Team Deathmatch but with fixed spawn points rather than ones that rotate around the map based on player position, it can lead to some particularly one-note matches. A brief invincibility window does prevent you from being gunned down straight away each time you spawn, but it doesn’t fully stop what I largely found to be a frustrating experience, whether you’re on the good or bad side of the deal. Either you’re well-positioned near the enemy spawn point and find yourself mindlessly shooting fish in a barrel or face the humiliation of running into a hail of bullets a few seconds after each death. It’s Edge of Tomorrow without any of the fun sci-fi story or Tom Cruise shouting at you.

Ground War is a returning mode that I also don’t ever have the desire to play. Large-scale 24v24 battles on huge maps full of tanks and other heavy vehicles with three points for your team to capture; it really is just a poor man’s Battlefield. Other than serving as a useful place to level up sniper rifles and RPGs, it’s not somewhere I go if I’m actually looking for a good time, as has been the case ever since its introduction in the 2019 reboot. I come to Call of Duty to play Call of Duty — fast-paced, small map action that I get a quick hit of dopamine from.

Modern Warfare 4 is at its best when it’s doing just that, building upon the sturdy foundations of what made the series the online multiplayer giant it is today. Whether that reminds us of the hours we lost in our teenage years to Deathmatch in Shipment, or innovates by remixing those memories through Kill Block’s novel approach to map design. I don’t come to Call of Duty to play poor imitations of Counter-Strike or Battlefield. It feels a little picky to complain about the sheer amount on offer, but it does feel like Infinity Ward is trying to have its cake and eat it too. I’d rather have one slice of amazing-tasting cake than bites of eight different ones if half haven’t been baked properly.

I’d be lying if I said I haven’t been having fun playing Modern Warfare 4, though. There’s enough good stuff here for me to focus on what I enjoy; it just so happens to be that outside of one map and one mode, all of that is stuff that existed years prior. It’s largely familiar, comfortable, and the thrill of unleashing a powerful killstreak in Deathmatch or pulling off a heroic comeback in Gunfight still hits as it should. The fundamentals are as strong as ever, but what’s new fails to build upon any of it in interesting ways. I’ll continue to play more over the next few days now that the public servers are live before locking in my fully scored verdict.

items.title: Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 Review
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Last year, Asus and Xbox worked together to launch the Asus ROG Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X, and the latter is still one of the best handheld gaming PCs on the market right now. Not only is is great at playing games, but even amid the RAMpocalypse, the Xbox Ally X hasn't gone up in price and will still cost the same $999 that it did back in October 2025.

While the Xbox Ally X is an incredible little device, its relatively small display has been outclassed by the likes of the Lenovo Legion Go 2 and MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ — even though they're more expensive. But Asus took the 20th anniversary of ROG to update the Xbox Ally X with an OLED display, and it takes the handheld to a completely new level.

With a better display and a new chassis comes a higher $1,299 price tag, but if you have the cash, that extra $300 is absolutely worth it.

Same Guts, Different Screen

The Xbox Ally X20 has a fancier looking chassis and a much nicer OLED display, but it's functionally the same handheld as the Ally X beneath the surface with no real difference in the specs. It's still rocking the AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme, along with 24GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. It shouldn't be too surprising that performance is largely the same, netting 42 fps in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p High settings with FSR set to Quality compared to 43 fps from the Xbox Ally X with the same settings.

In 3DMark, the performance also lines up. The Xbox Ally X20 gets 598 points in the Steel Nomad test, compared to 602 points from the original Xbox Ally X, which is within the margin of error. In Time Spy, the X20 gets 4,030 points, compared to 4,016 points from last year's model — also virtually the same performance.

Of course, because OLED displays are slightly more efficient than your standard LCD screen, the Xbox Ally X20's battery fares a bit better than its predecessor. Starting from 100% battery, I played Cyberpunk 2077 until the X20 died, and it lasted 2 hours and 43 minutes with all stock settings. That makes it the longest lasting handheld I've tested, beating out the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+'s 2 hours and 14 minutes, and the Xbox Ally X's 2 hours and 34 minutes. You're only getting an extra 10 minutes of battery life, so it's not exactly groundbreaking, but it an improvement.

If you already have the Xbox Ally X, it's not worth upgrading to the X20 based on specs alone. But the star of the show is the improved OLED display.

OLED Makes a World of Difference

While I still love the original Xbox Ally X, the display has always been a problem for me. In a lot of games, especially as time has gone on, I've found myself needing to squint at the screen in dark scenes to make out what's happening. Likewise, in games like Monster Hunter Rise (which I've unfortunately found myself recently obssessed with), the original Ally X's screen isn't great at making the bright colors pop off the screen as well as an OLED display can.

For a long time, that led me to daily driving the Lenovo Legion Go 2, which has its own problems. I have pretty small hands, and there are times where I struggle to stretch my thumb to hit all of the buttons. Plus, with all the dials and buttons built into the Joy-Con-like controllers on the Legion Go 2, it's easy to accidentally hit something and trick the game into thinking you're playing with a keyboard and mouse, even for just a second. But because the screen is so good, I would just power through, and it's become one of the default ways I play games in bed, whether it's something that's running locally on the Legion Go 2 or streaming through Moonlight.

After spending a few days with the Xbox Ally X20, I've shoved the Legion Go 2 back into storage. The X20's screen is smaller, but it's much easier to hold for long periods of time, which completely equalizes it for me. Plus, the crystal-clear display makes it easier to see whatever's on the screen, so having less real estate there doesn't make much of a difference.

While the new OLED display is the highlight, the Xbox Ally X20 also has a new, partially transparent chassis that's evocative of '90s gadget design. It does look great, even if I prefer the simple black aesthetic of the original. The menu buttons are all gold now, which is apparently the standard color of 'anniversary' or 'celebration' editions of tech products, and other buttons, like the volume rocker and all the standard controller inputs, are black.

What's more interesting is the D-pad. Asus worked in a transforming D-pad that you can pull out and rotate to transform it from a classically defined pad with four directional buttons to a concave version akin to what you'd find on the Xbox Elite controllers. A lot of controller makers do offer this choice, but it's usually handled by having a removable D-pad rather than one that can transform. If you do have a preference for one type of pad, you can set it that way, but really, I've just been fidgeting with it because of the satisfying clicking noise it makes whenever you pull it out and rotate it.

The sticks have also been updated from the standard sticks on the Xbox Ally X to new TMR sensors on the X20. Day to day, that difference hasn't been noticeable for me, but it does mean that they should last much longer without stick drift. That's super important in a device where, if the controller breaks, you can't easily swap out the controller or its parts without taking the whole thing apart.

Unfortunately, It's Still Running Windows

Just like any other handheld, what really holds the Xbox Ally X20 back from greatness is the software. Windows 11 is still a pain to use with a controller, and while the Xbox Full Screen Experience does mitigate many of the problems, there are still some definite issues.

In the few days I've spent with the Xbox Ally X20, I've run into one specific problem over and over again: If I try to swipe up on the display to go to another window, the controller will bug out. It acts as though the Xbox button is being held down, which means every button press is read as a shortcut, either opening the keyboard, pulling up the task manager, or some other silly behavior. It's bad enough when I'm trying to scroll through my library, but when I'm trying to pull up a guide in a browser and swap back and forth, it makes the X20 unusable until I reboot the thing.

To be fair, the original Xbox Ally X had problems with the Full Screen Experience when it launched, too. But that was when it was and none of the problems were as toxic to the experience as making the controller essentially non-functional. I've been able to get around these problems with the X20's UI by avoiding using the touchscreen as much as possible, but that's not something I should have to do with a $1,300 device, especially when it's essentially just a chassis and display upgrade.

This should be something that future updates should be able to fix, but in the meantime, I'd advise forgoing Windows and installing SteamOS or Bazzite, unless you really want to use it to play Game Pass games or Call of Duty.

Looking at what is essentially a PC version of the Nintendo Switch 2 and seeing a $1,299 price tag is going to turn some people off from the jump, but I'm still surprised that this handheld is as affordable as it is. The Xbox Ally X20 has nearly the same specs as the Lenovo Legion Go 2, except with 8GB less of RAM, but it costs $700 less at the time of writing.

It's not hard to look at other PC gaming hardware this year and imagine that Asus could have raised the price more, considering the much-improved display and the addition of TMR joysticks. Just look at the Steam Machine, which came in at $1,049, or even the 4-year-old Steam Deck, which Valve bumped up to $789 back in May. Compared to the Xbox Ally X20's Z2 Extreme, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD, the Steam Deck's aging RDNA 2 GPU, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB SSD at nearly $800 doesn't seem like that great of a deal at all.

Crucially, Asus also isn't discontinuing the existing Xbox Ally X, which is still a $999 handheld despite the price increases that have hit pretty much every other tech product this year. I keep bracing myself for what feels like the inevitability that Asus is going to raise its prices, but that hasn't happened yet. Now Asus is launching a new version of the Xbox Ally X, but with an OLED panel and TMR sticks for $1,299. That upgrade be a bit cheaper, but it's hard to think of a single handheld gaming PC with an OLED display that is a better value right now.

items.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Episodes 4-6 Recap and Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
With the next batch of three episodes of Avatar: Seven Havens now on Paramount+, we’re nearly halfway through the first season of the series. The show has clearly hit an episodic rhythm and is amping up the danger for our twin Avatars, Pavi (Saheli Kahn) and Nisha (Aishu Devan), as well as their supposed safe Haven of Ellora. But we’re also in Ellora, and other than a very menacing red diamond and a group of raiders called the Faceless, it’s curious that we still don’t quite have a sense of what the overall thrust of this story is as of yet.

Okay, that’s not true; the thrust of Book 1: Survival (the overarching name for the season) certainly seems to be Pavi and Nisha regaining the lost memories of their past while the tensions and distrust in Ellora bubble over to unbearable levels, mostly focused on the unseen threat of the Avatar — after all, we’re told it was the previous Avatar, Korra, who broke the world two centuries ago, leading to what’s left of humanity living in Seven Havens.

But the real tense question for viewers watching the show is: When are they going to leave this One (1) Haven and explore the other Six (6) Havens, to make Seven total Havens? Look, it’s gotta happen — probably — but this isn’t the single-city focus that mostly consumed Legend of Korra. There, it made sense to spend a lot of time in Republic City; the steampunk-inspired home for all four types of benders and humans was a vast array of landscapes and social strata. Ellora, by design, is smaller and more in line with where we first met Aang with the Southern Water Tribe before heading off to explore the wide world of Avatar.

In fact, if you look at a similar span of time on The Last Airbender, team Avatar had left the Southern Water Tribe by Episode 6, went to the Southern Air Temple, met the Kyoshi Warriors, headed to the Earth Kingdom of Omashu, and fought the at-the-time villainous Zuko multiple times. Not that Seven Havens needs to ape that formula, but the curiosity factor about the new landscape of the world after Korra’s cataclysm (Korraclysm?) is high. We end Episode 6, “Night of the Afflicted,” with Ellora calling the other Havens for help; however, that likely means the other Havens are coming to Ellora, not Pavi and Nisha going to them.

The show is lovely to look at on an episode-by-episode basis, adorably funny, and doing a nice job of slowly fleshing out the expansive cast.

This would be much less of a problem if every episode didn’t include the twins talking about how they want to go find their parents and see if they’re alive. Yet not once does anyone say, “okay, let’s check Ellora,” which is the last place they were seen. Yes, Ellora and its citizens are getting plenty of time in the sun, and they’re all interesting in their own right. But at this point, it feels like Seven Havens is fighting against itself to keep our characters in town instead of following the quest structure the season seemed to be setting up.

Those five paragraphs aside, let’s not also forget that this is a very fun show and a great addition to the Avatar canon. While the season-long view raises some questions about the show’s direction, it’s still lovely to look at on an episode-by-episode basis, adorably funny, and doing a nice job of slowly fleshing out the expansive cast. And out of New York Comic Con that the show will now run at least four seasons, there’s a little bit more breathing room for Seven Havens to stay in Ellora before Pavi, Nisha, and presumably Jae (Major Curda) head out to repair this broken world. When they had just announced two seasons, you could hear the clock ticking away in the background; now, they can hang in Ellora for Season 1 but hopefully get on the road in Seasons 2-4.

Okay, enough long view. To break down the plot more specifically, Episode 4, “The Faceless,” focuses on what seemed to be the big threat last week. As it turns out, they’re really raiders taking grain and other goods from Ellora — late in the episode they kidnap a herd of cameldillos. The smart thing this half-hour does is take this threat and pair it with a very small, personal quest for our three leads to find missing Bending Brigade member Uki (Kimberly Woods). Not only does this allow Pavi to get weirder, building on her “actually, I talk to rocks and they’re my friends” moment from Episode 3, but it gives us more of a chance to understand the increased fear and panic in Ellora that’s caused or amplified by what was left behind by the red diamond.

Not to compare and contrast two extremely different shows, but take a look at Lanterns over on HBO, which spent a lot of time telling us how nervous the people of the town of Rushville, Nebraska were, while only showing us those people one or two times in eight episodes. Meanwhile, Seven Havens depicts this on multiple levels, from those in the ruling class to citizens in a delicious looking bakery to Uki’s insanely large family, who are worried not just about her but the city itself. As viewers, this gives us a specific emotional tie versus Pavi and Nisha riding their cat-monkeys through a town of, er, faceless nobodies. This storyline is all about panic and fear of the unknown, something relevant to our modern world. The almost-riot in Episode 5, “The One Left Behind,” and the pseudo-zombie attacks in Episode 6, “Night of the Afflicted,” wouldn’t be as effective if we didn’t care about the regular people of Ellora.

And now a quick side-trip to theory town (and scroll down for a big theory that borders on possible spoilers): We’re all agreed that the Faceless aren’t bad guys; they’re people trying to survive outside the Haven, right? And given the “you should join us” moment at the beginning of the episode, by the time Jae finds Uki again, she’ll understand the Faceless point of view? Okay, cool.

To jump into Episode 5, now that city guard Molin (Osric Chau) is possessed by the red entity and knows (or thinks he knows) the Avatar is in town, tensions are unbearably high. What works nicely about the animation here is that the expressions convey the real pain and terror everyone is feeling as the Guards work to track down the Avatar. Meanwhile, Jae and Bending Brigade Commander Karthik (Akshay Khanna) try to alleviate fears despite knowing there isn’t just one but Avatars in Ellora.

There’s a lot to like about this episode. Shouts to Seven Havens for doubling down on the relationship between Jae and Datu (Topher Ngo). There’s the funniest moment they’ve had so far, with an old woman responding to Jae’s impassioned pleas with a raspberry, then being haughtily carried away by a large man. And of course, Karthik has a secret closet full of artifacts, aka Avatar easter eggs, which we’ll get into more after the recap. But the biggest plus is again keeping things focused on emotion while spooling out the plot. Here, thanks to a rediscovered bracelet paired with Pavi’s brooch, we discover that Nisha and Pavi’s parents were trying to hide them and contacted the Order of the White Lotus, but when Karthik arrived, he only found Nisha alone in the wasteland. There are strong shades of Rey’s story from Star Wars: The Last Jedi here, though clearly our twin Avatars’ parents know a whole lot more about the world breaking than we’re aware of at the moment.

And then there’s Episode 6, which has Ellora getting its fears amplified by the crystalline structures left behind by the red diamond, with the evil diamond returning not to attack but to show Pavi and Nisha another vision of their mother and father. Perhaps most importantly, Pavi calms down Molin by sticking him in a “cozy wall,” which counts as number two after Raspberry Lady in the list of funniest moments in this batch of episodes. Not to sound like a broken record, but once again this episode pairs the fear zombie plot (the big story) with Pavi’s own fears that she won’t be good enough thanks to the loss of her leg (ostensibly the little story). There’s clearly more to tell there, but the animation conveys her pain and frustration as she tries to help Nisha and Jae quell the madness, and the ultimate delivery of a new prosthetic from an kindly doctor is joyful, as Pavi bounces around the room.

As with The Last Airbender and later seasons of The Legend of Korra, the focus is on characters and emotion first.

Naturally, the mysteries here — Why are there Avatars? What’s up with the red diamond? Is it really the wrath of the spirit world, or something else? What about those other six Havens? — are great to theorize about. But as with The Last Airbender and later seasons of The Legend of Korra (they made the mistake of going a little too plot- and exposition-heavy in the first season), the focus is on characters and emotion .

This does tie neatly into The Big Theory we’ll get into below, and while there is a bit of the “when are they going to get to the fireworks factory” in regards to those other Six Havens in this week’s batch of episodes, Seven Havens is doing a bang-up job of making us care not just about Pavi and Nisha, but all of Ellora. There’s a kindness and empathy running through this series that is rare even for animated shows. In short? Avatar: Seven Havens is like sitting inside a nice, cozy wall for 60ish minutes every week.

Avatar Easter Eggs, References, And Connections

Before we get into specific easter eggs, here’s that theory we mentioned — and while it just a fan theory posted on , it’s the sort of thing that feels so correct, it may have figured out the whole show after the first week. So possible future spoilers on: The Seven Havens are the Seven Chakras. That’s the short version, but if you don’t recall — back in The Last Airbender Season 2, Aang learned about the seven chakras that, when unlocked, allow him to enter the all-powerful Avatar State. He initially was unable to unlock them due to not letting go of attachments, and was later badly hurt due to Azula’s lightning bending.

Each chakra has a color and an associated emotion, and the colors of the Seven Havens all coincide with the colors of the various chakras. Ellora, you may not be surprised to learn, is depicted as red in the opening credits, and the red chakra or Root Chakra, is blocked by fear. The title of the season finale of Seven Havens’ first season? “The Root Chakra.”

While not exactly “case closed,” the theory continues that Korra either did something or was trying to prevent something from happening (and failed) that broke the chakras of the world. So once Pavi and Nisha figure this out, they won’t be going on a journey to figure out bending à la Aang and Korra since they’ve already mastered all four elements, but rather to unlock the seven chakras of the world and restore balance. The weird weather? That’s because the chakras are blocked; it would also explain why the red diamond isn’t evil. It just needs Pavi and Nisha to do something to unblock Ellora’s fear.

If this is indeed a journey to restore the chakras, the place where Korra probably made her last stand would definitely be her home from Legend of Korra.

One additional aspect of this theory, by the way, is that intrepid fans have already laid the map of the Seven Havens from the opening credits over the known map of the Avatar world. While some places are unknown or guesses, it seems almost a given that one of the Havens is Ba Sing Se, while the likely final one is none other than Republic City. Again, this makes a lot of sense; if this is indeed a journey to restore the chakras, the place where Korra probably made her last stand would definitely be her home from Legend of Korra.

Is this all true? Just wild guesses? We’ll find out as the show continues, but let’s get into some easter eggs and references we know for sure.

To work backwards (because pretty much everything we need to talk about is in Episode 5), it’s neat to see lightning bending again, aka the coolest bending. We also get to see Pavi and Nisha do energy bending to “banish” the red diamond, which stuns Karthik. While the above Big Theory seems more plausible, this could throw a little more fire on the “Aang did something when he removed Fire Lord Ozai’s bending” theory, since that also involved energy bending.

Okay, fine, Episode 5. Right at the beginning, we get a fun little mention of “Commander Bountan once told me he saw a dancing lemur-man in the harshlands.” While there’s no way Bountan actually saw this, it’s clear this is a reference to Momo’s iconic dancing in The Last Airbender Season 2, “Tales of Ba Sing Se,” where he danced with some monkeys while trying to find the missing Appa.

…And then Pavi and Nisha end up in Karthik’s secret room, a treasure trove of artifacts collected by the Order of the White Lotus. Look, full disclosure: We’re definitely going to miss things here because there is , so sound off in the comments below if you catch something we don’t. But a partial list of artifacts includes:

  • Sokka’s club, which Pavi uses as a backscratcher and pulls a classic Sokka face as she does
  • It looks like they might also have Sokka’s sword on one of the higher shelves
  • A fan from one of the Kyoshi Warriors
  • The Avatar Relics, aka the toys used to identify Avatars. At the very least, there’s the hand drum, wooden hog monkey, and pull-string propeller used with Aang seen in the foreground as Nisha enters the room
  • The map of the world as seen in the opening title sequence of The Last Airbender
  • Zuko’s Blue Spirit mask from when he went undercover as a vigilante
  • Nisha picks up an object with the three swirls indicating the Air Nation
  • There’s a musical instrument on the wall that, shapewise, looks closest to Chong’s instrument — the dramyin — from The Last Airbender Season 2’s “The Cave of Two Lovers”
  • Any radios are going to be from the Legend of Korra era, since the tech hadn’t been developed in the time of The Last Airbender. It’s possible one of these might be Bumi’s portable radio, or based on it in some way
  • As Pavi accidentally turns on the radio and becomes terrified, we see a red umbrella, which is likely the same one Aang got as a present in The Last Airbender Season 1, Episode 14, “The Fortuneteller”

The “lantern” Pavi excitedly calls out definitely seems to be something, so feel free to make fun of us for not figuring out what it is; same for the purple robe with long sleeves in the back, which looks like something Princess Yue would wear but is not. Probably. Regardless, there’s a there to freeze frame and comb through, and it makes sense that they wouldn’t have many relics from Korra’s era since they, you know, Korra.

items.title: Sacrifice Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Sacrifice hits Netflix on October 16.

Isn’t it nice when Netflix puts out a decent movie? Yes, the streaming juggernaut releases high quality efforts from auteurs like and , but then there’s the neverending parade of , mediocrity; mostly paper thin comedy-action films with forgettable plots and vapid characters, whose only strengths come from the charisma of the actors playing them. At this point, Chris Evans is one of many likable actors who has made a few of these types of movies now, for multiple streamers, so it’s easy to assume Sacrifice will be another example. Yet lo and behold, this one actually feels like something with more commendable aspirations.

Evans plays movie star Mike Tyler here, attending a climate charity event on a Greek island while attempting a comeback after a public meltdown a year earlier. However, the event is interrupted by a cult-like group of radicals, led by Joan (Anya Taylor-Joy), who take everyone hostage at gunpoint.

And then… things actually go quite differently than you’d expect from a Netflix movie with this set-up and these stars. Because it’s incredibly easy to imagine the version of Sacrifice where Evans’ Mike must rise to the occasion, putting his movie star training into real world use… for halfhearted comedy-action hijinks.

But director and co-screenwriter Romain Gavras and his co-screenwriter, Will Arbery, have something more cerebral in mind. So while there are comedic moments to the film, especially early on, the story is actually focused on Mike as a man adrift – well aware of the performative nature of the rich, famous and powerful people he’s among – and what happens when he comes face to face with a group of genuine, albeit most certainly violent, activists.

While there are comedic moments to the film, especially early on, the story is actually focused on Evans' Mike as a man adrift.

Mike is one of three partygoers, along with billionaire Ben (Vincent Cassel) and performer Katie (Ambika Mod), to be chosen by Joan and her group for a supposed sacrifice in order to stop what they believe to be the imminent end of the world in just two days. This combination of a doomsday-prophet-on-a-mission story with an eat the rich hostage scenario ultimately feels somewhat like an enticing combination of this year’s Sam Rockwell-led Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die and another Anya Taylor-Joy movie, .

The journey that follows takes a lot of notable turns, as Mike begins to be drawn to the self-assured Joan and her absolute certainty in herself and what her mission is. And again, thankfully, Mike’s privileged movie star background isn’t used for just the jokey “get a load of this blowhard” approach it could be, but rather for something more introspective and thoughtful…

…Well, mostly. Because there are still some mannered, would-be pop-culture-skewing moments included, mostly via cutaways to some of the media attention the hostage story is getting or through Mike’s agent, Oliver (Sam Richardson). But as the story continues, these “wackier” scenes feel increasingly like a distracting, disconnected element that exists outside the central story.

Produced independently – Netflix picked it up following film festival screenings – Sacrifice has a strong visual approach thanks to music video veteran Gavras and cinematographer Matias Boucard. There are some great shots of the film’s island setting, nearby volcano included, and Gavras is among the directors who has realized that Taylor-Joy’s unique features, shot in a stark closeup (including straight to camera), make for a stirring cinematic image in their own right, particularly when the actress is playing a determined character such as Joan.

Sacrifice doesn’t quite accomplish all it’s setting out to do, and despite strong work from Evans and Taylor-Joy, the characters are more archetypes than richly detailed. But they work well for what they are and in their depiction of two very different people on this odd and unexpected journey together.

Those out of place, heightened comedy segments aside, the film is actually quite strange and melancholy in an inviting way, backed by an atmospheric score by Gener8ion and cool song choices like Leonard Cohen’s “Who By Fire” (meanwhile, Charli xcx pops up early on at the charity event, singing a tongue in cheek song about helping the environment).

Cassel has some strong moments as the arrogant Ben, while Yung Lean and Jade Croot both convey the right attitude as Joan’s likeminded siblings and partners. John Malkovich is a great casting get as Joan’s father (Malkovich and Taylor-Joy as father and daughter just seems right), though he feels underutilized. Salma Hayek Pinault has some fun moments early on as Ben’s wife, though the character feels somewhat forgotten about as the film progresses.

items.title: Street Fighter Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
There’s an infectious and celebratory energy coursing through Kitao Sakurai’s Street Fighter at every turn… Psycho Power, you could say. And “Psycho Power” is an apt metaphysical concept to have so front-and-center of the movie’s plot, because as Capcom’s roster of colorful and strange lowercase “c” combatants strut their stuff and pull off their special moves in hyperkinetic fashion, the movie increasingly feels disconnected from any sense of reality, even its own. Is that really a problem when you’ve got martial arts warriors and demons throwing fireballs, green monsters with Jason Momoa’s face rolling around, or Eric Andre screaming through a bullhorn at the top of his lungs? As it turns out, yes. But, as you quickly learn while watching it, Street Fighter never lets good sense get in the way of a good time.

Street Fighter gets off to a stylish start with a wonderfully executed anime prologue that sets up the divide between protagonists Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken (Noah Centineo), martial artists who’d grown to be best friends while training under their master Gouken (Don Lee). As Ryu fades into obscurity, Ken becomes a pop culture mainstay who can never quite shake the idea that his former friend was the better fighter after Ryu demonstrates an ability to harness “Hado power.” That mystical energy from the spirit realm is only able to be channeled by the greatest warriors, and Sakurai and co-writer T.J. Fixman devote about as many words in their script to explaining it as are included in this very sentence.

More necessary to the plot is how important this ability is to M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), the sadistic leader of the Shadaloo crime organization who stages a tournament of the world’s greatest fighters in hopes of sapping enough Hado power (or Psycho Power, as it’s called around Bison’s office) for him to unlock special moves of his very own. Street Fighter makes a bet that scant few in its audience are going to give two rips about how well-justified its melting pot of characters, magic abilities, and cultural influences winds up, with Sakurai seeming far more intent on representing the franchise as broadly as possible at the cost of telling a deeper story.

The fast and loose nature of the adaptation’s storytelling relies heavily on expected genre tropes for both Ryu and Ken, and that effort falls frustratingly short of how good both Andrew Koji and Noah Centineo are in their respective roles. Between the two, Centineo’s Ken gets more latitude to demonstrate how his attention-starved tenure in Ryu’s shadow has affected him, and Centineo’s restlessness gives Ken a fun “little brother” energy that feels like it goes a lot further to propping up his underdog status within the story than the actual writing of the character does. Ken’s reasons for staying locked into the tournament are never quite clear: Is he here to prove himself against Ryu? To honor his master? To save himself from more MTV Spring Break appearances? To save? Maybe for supporting characters, those reasons are less important. But as one of the two leads and certainly the one with more time in the spotlight, Ken’s motivation could have used a lot more focus, which would’ve allowed for his struggles later in the movie to hit home with the emotional weight the finale seems to be making space for.

Each performer brings inherent strengths to the roles which make up a lot of ground for how underwritten many of them are.

Ryu’s arc has the inverse problem, with a poorly maintained throughline about his struggle with a dark power hiding just under the surface of his otherwise peaceful demeanor. He’s reluctant to engage with the tournament as a result, with that struggle embodied by Roman Reigns’ demonic Akuma, the games character which Street Fighter goes furthest out of its way to justify bringing into the fold here. As great as the Ryu/Ken anime scenes look, Sakurai flashes back to them more and more, which becomes a distracting crutch the movie uses to double back on itself and explain Akuma’s significance to Ryu and Ken’s early days.

It’s a shame, as Andrew Koji is quite compelling as Ryu and does great work keeping the character’s stoicism from drifting into feeling wooden, as often happens with action leads. With how cartoonishly emotive the other characters are, Ryu’s calm is a welcome contrast to whatever weirdo he’s paired up with in any given scene. Perhaps unsurprisingly, Ryu’s intense focus is best juxtaposed against Ken’s manic enthusiasm, and Koji and Centineo are each at their best when bickering with each other. An early fight between the two in a hotel room synthesizes that dynamic best in both performance and action, as Ryu’s one-upsmanship in the duel drives Ken increasingly up a wall. That relatively straightforward fight, and the precise nature of how the camera chases the choreography to accentuate comedic beats, is a bit of an outlier for Street Fighter because the rest of the fights are textbook examples of unchecked maximalism.

Street Fighter never lets too long go by without a brawl breaking out. Whether or not those brawls have any good reason to be happening, the movie certainly kicks into a higher gear when fists are flying, even if the tournament that acts as the backbone of the movie’s second half is pretty much an afterthought. The action blends Hong Kong, anime, and ’80s/’90s movie influences that alternatingly emphasize tight fight choreography and epic hero moments. In that way, ironically, that leaves Scott Pilgrim vs. The World’s video game-inspired action as the closest cinematic relative to Street Fighter’s, a similarity that also makes its way into how the movie’s comedic bent leaves that action needing to function as an engine for both adrenaline and laughs. Sakurai opts for a scattershot approach here, with a tendency to pack action scenes so full with individual gags that often there’s not enough time to fully appreciate them before he’s moving on to the next one. The action is very well-performed by the stunt team and those in the cast like Andrew Koji who are capable of handling the more complicated sequences themselves, but the plot does leave Street Fighter relying more on VFX embellishments to that action as it goes, which add very little to how viscerally it all lands.

The movie’s wide scope does lead to a pretty strong showing from the games’ deep bench of fighters, and the flavor each of their personalities bring to this whacked-out stew are the undeniable highlight of the movie. Through its first half, Street Fighter bends over backwards to introduce game characters like Chun-Li (Callina Liang), Guile (Cody Rhodes), Vega (Orville Peck), Dhalsim (Vidyut Jammwal), and Cammy (Mel Jarnson) and to keep them in the mix as the tournament begins in MetroLao City. These characters’ personal reasons for accepting their invitations become wholly irrelevant after they’re in the door, but Street Fighter is no weaker for that. With no responsibilities to the plot, these fighters are given license to be as bizarre and funny as their individual performers can sustain, and the characters that leave a mark really leave a mark.

Andrew Schulz’s Dan Hibiki, Ken’s replacement best friend after Ryu disappears, is the big surprise on that front. As Ken’s agent, Dan begins the story looking like a money-hungry leech, but his genuine care for his buddy actually becomes one of the few emotional hooks that the movie’s got by the end, and Schulz plays being out of his depth around people who could rock his shit to frequently funny effect. Another comedian who sees big success throughout Street Fighter is Eric Andre, whose emcee Don Sauvage is essentially just a thinly veiled spin on his own signature chaos energy.

From the moment Cody Rhodes’ Guile enters (hair first, of course) to the tune of his absolutely rocking theme song, the strength of his all-American charisma and consistent ability to nail punchlines are let down only by the relatively brief amount of screentime he gets. Others — like Balrog or Zangief — are glorified cameos that at least each add a unique energy to their scenes. Jason Momoa’s Blanka certainly falls into this camp: He’s barely involved, but dang it if the freakish CGI and “Hulked on Phonics” speech pattern that define him don’t leave you leaning in with amused bewilderment by the time he rolls out of the movie. David Dastmalchian’s M. Bison is another reliable source of amusing bewilderment that Street Fighter draws on to great effect: Bison’s relationship to power and just how… gratified he becomes as he creeps closer and closer to attaining it is a surprisingly off-kilter approach to the imposing dictator, and one that Dastmalchian never blinks in the face of.

These characters really exemplify the importance of good casting, as each performer brings inherent strengths to the roles which make up a lot of ground for how underwritten many of them are. That lack of definition does backfire with the most prominent female characters: Callina Liang’s Chun-Li and Mel Jarnson’s Cammy are certainly pretty high up on the list of historically overly sexualized video game characters, a fact Street Fighter doesn’t have an intelligent enough take on to poke fun at without just perpetuating it further. But whether it’s a character rooted in strong cinematic archetypes like Guile or unfortunate ones like Chun-Li, all of the performers wholeheartedly embrace the movie’s ridiculous tone and keep it afloat when the writing lets them down. Street Fighter’s 1990s setting is supposed to be another source of campy energy for the movie, but Sakurai never quite figures out how to effectively channel that nostalgia — little of the production design feels that demonstrative of the period, leaving the way-too-frequent needle drops (including one that released on the whole other end of the decade in which the movie’s set) doing all the heavy lifting on that score.

items.title: SanDisk MicroSD Express Review: Super-Fast Storage for Your Switch 2
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
If you care about raw throughput when picking a microSD Express card, SanDisk’s officially-licensed microSD Express Card for Nintendo Switch 2 may be the one to beat. I’ve been testing one for the last week, and in almost every test I threw at it, it outdid IGN’s current budget pick for the best Nintendo Switch 2 microSD Express card, the Samsung P9 Express.

The real question is whether that’s even worth paying for. MicroSD Express cards are already very fast compared to the older microSD ones still used on every gaming handheld that’s not the Switch 2, and it’s not even close. SanDisk’s card is demonstrably faster in many ways than competing options from PNY and Samsung, but unless you’re transferring game files back and forth between it and your Switch 2, you’re really not going to notice. Faster better, but there are other things to consider, including price.

SanDisk offers its card in 256GB, 512GB, and 1TB capacities. I’ve found 512GB to be the sweet spot, giving you three quarters of a terabyte overall when you factor in the console’s internal 256GB storage. But SanDisk’s cards cost more than similar options from PNY or Walmart’s Onn brand.

When you’re looking at the specs for a microSD Express card for Switch 2, you can safely ignore the main throughput numbers that most manufacturers like to promote. In the case of SanDisk’s card, that’s 880 MB/s reads and 650MB/s writes, which is faster than almost all the other cards I’ve tested! (The only one rated higher is the PNY one, at 890MB/s and 750MB/s, respectively.) But that number refers to the read figure, and as my testing showed, is a poor reflection of actual performance during the reads and writes.

See, video games aren’t monolithic files; they’re packages containing countless smaller files so the process of transferring them is constantly starting and stopping, slowing things significantly. How well a card performs there depends on how it handles these herky-jerky transfers.

Getting a handle on a microSD Express card’s Switch 2 throughput means timing file transfers between it and my console in docked mode. And in that, SanDisk’s card proved super capable. For instance, it reached 94 MB/s when writing Mario Kart World, currently a 22GB game (versus 21.9GB when I tested for the Samsung P9 Express before) to the card. It was actually slightly when it came to moving games back to the Switch 2’s internal storage, only mustering 91MB/s.

That played out the same way for every game I tested. It averaged 105MB/s when I transferred Resident Evil 4 to the card and just 80MB/s on the way back to the console, and I measured 95MB/s to the card and 85MB/s from it when moving Super Smash Bros. back and forth. The 8.9GB Donkey Kong Bananza was the fastest one; it took just over a minute to write the 8.9GB game to the card, making its throughput 122MB/s. (It averaged 88MB/s when I sent it back to internal storage.)

Despite yielding slower reads than writes, SanDisk’s card still outperformed most other cards I’ve tested in most cases. Samsung’s card put up a higher 96MB/s when I transferred Resident Evil 4 from it to my Switch 2 but otherwise ranged between about 1MB/s to 12MB/s slower on other games. The PNY card put up mostly similar read speeds, but managed closer to half the writes of the SanDisk option when it came to write speeds. That could be a difference of minutes on larger files — Mario Kart World took over seven minutes to write to PNY’s card, something that only took about four minutes with SanDisk’s. Basically, if you find yourself shuffling games on and off your Switch 2, the SanDisk microSD Express card could save you real time.

Things equalize where it’s most important: actual loading times for games. Measuring these, I found that the SanDisk card looked almost exactly the same as both the PNY and Samsung cards I tested before. Donkey Kong Bananza took 21 seconds to go from choosing it on the Switch 2’s home screen to its title screen, just like those cards. Mario Kart World averaged 19.4 seconds, or a tenth of a second behind the PNY card and about two seconds faster than the Samsung P9. It got me into The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom nearly a full second faster, at 8.5 seconds, than either of those cards, though.

It’s clear that SanDisk’s officially-licensed Switch 2 card is at least as good as the other high-performing cards on the market, so you won’t be disappointed. It’s still slower than loading games from the Switch 2’s internal storage for the most part, but the difference is negligible – most games only load a fraction of a second faster from the Switch 2 itself than from microSD Express.

items.title: South Park Season 29, Episode 3 Review & Recap: 'You Like That on Your Face'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for South Park Season 29, Episode 3!

Yeesh, that was probably the weakest new episode of South Park in several years. As is often the case in the show's lesser moments, "You Like That on Your Face" has a few amusing gags and ideas, but none of it comes together as a cohesive whole. Talk about cringe...
